(Surah of the Mother of the Qur'an)

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ The preposition bāʾ (bāʾ al-jarr) comes with several meanings: attachment (lil-ilṣāq), seeking help (lil-istiʿānah), oath (lil-qasam), cause (lil-sababiyyah), accompaniment or circumstance (lil-ḥāl), locative sense (lil-ẓarfiyyah), and transference (lil-naql). Attachment in its literal sense: "I wiped my head" (masaḥtu bi-raʾsī); in a figurative sense: "I passed by Zayd" (marartu bi-Zayd). Seeking help: "I slaughtered with the knife" (dhabaḥtu bi-l-sikkīn). Cause: ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them [certain good things]﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 160]. Oath: "By Allah, he has certainly stood up" (bi-Llāhi la-qad qāma). Circumstance: "Zayd came with his garments" (jāʾa Zayd bi-thiyābihi). Locative: "Zayd is in Basra" (Zayd bi-l-Baṣrah). Transference: "I stood up with Zayd" (qumtu bi-Zayd). It also comes as an emphatic extra particle (zāʾidah lil-tawkīd): "They drank from the water of the sea" (shariban bi-māʾi l-baḥr); as a substitute (lil-badal): "Would that I had instead of them a people" (falayta lī bihim qawman), i.e., instead of them; as an exchange (lil-muqābalah): "I bought the horse for a thousand" (ishtaraytu l-faras bi-alf); as a sense of passing beyond (lil-mujāwazah): ﴿The sky will be split open by the clouds﴾ [al-Furqān: 25], i.e., "from" the clouds; and as elevation (lil-istiʿlāʾ): ﴿Of them is one who, if you entrust him with a qintār﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 75]. Some scholars expressed the circumstantial sense by accompaniment, adding that it may also denote causation, and expressed seeking help by cause, and the circumstantial sense by the meaning of maʿa (with), in agreement with the meaning of the lām.

It is said: ism, with the hamzat al-waṣl pronounced with kasra or damma; sim, with the sīn pronounced with kasra or damma; and sumā, like hudā. The Basrī grammarians say its root consists of sīn, mīm and wāw, while the Kufī grammarians say it is wāw, sīn and mīm; the stronger view is the first, and the proof is found in the books of grammar.

The definite article al- (alif-lām) is used for previous mention of a specific person or of a genus (lil-ʿahd fī shakhṣ aw jins), for presence (lil-ḥuḍūr), for singling out a quality (lil-lamḥ al-ṣifah), for dominance (lil-ghalabah), and as a relative (mawṣūlah). For previous mention of a specific person: "The boy came" (jāʾa al-ghulām); of a genus: "Give me water" (usqinī al-māʾ); for presence: "I went out and behold, the lion" (fa-idhā al-asad); for singling out: "al-Ḥārith"; for dominance: "al-Dabarān." It is also an inseparable extra (zāʾidah lāzimah) and a non-inseparable extra (ghayr lāzimah): the inseparable one is like in "al-ān" (now); the non-inseparable one is as in the verse:

"He distanced Umm al-ʿAmr from her captive."

Is it composed of two letters or is it a single letter? And if it is of two letters, is the hamzah an extra or not? There are various views, and God knows best. The name (Allah) is not applied except to the One truly worshipped; it is an original proper noun (murtajal), not derived, according to most scholars. It was said to be derived; its root is said to be lām, yāʾ and hāʾ, from lāha yalīhi, meaning "he rose high." It is said that for this reason the sun was called ilāhah, with kasra or fatḥa on the hamzah. It was also said that its root is lām, wāw and hāʾ, from lāha yalūhu lawhan, meaning "he veiled himself or shone"; its weight at that time would be faʿala or faʿila. It was also said that the alif is extra and its root is hamzah and lām, from aliha, meaning "he was alarmed," as said by Ibn Isḥāq; or allaha, meaning "he was bewildered," as said by Abū ʿUmar; or allaha, meaning "he worshipped," as said by al-Naḍr; or aliha, meaning "he became calm," as said by al-Mubarrad. According to these views, the hamzah was dropped by ʿitibāṭ (a regular dropping), as it is said of nās, whose origin is unās; or it was dropped for transference, and the lām remained with idghām (assimilation); both opinions are anomalous. It was also said that its root is wāw, lām and hāʾ, from walaha, meaning "he was enraptured," and the hamzah in it was changed from wāw, like ashāḥa; this was said by al-Khalīl and al-Qannād, but it is weak because the substitution is obligatory. As for their plural āliha, the word may also be fiʿāl in the sense of maf ʿūl, like kitāb meaning "that which is written." As for the alif-lām in Allah, when we say its origin is al-Ilāh, they say it is for dominance, since al-Ilāh is applied to the one worshipped in truth and in falsehood, whereas Allah is applied only to the one worshipped in truth; so it became like al-najm for al-Thurayyā. It is objected that it is not like al-najm, because after the deletion and transference or assimilation it was no longer applied to every deity, and then it became specific to the one worshipped in truth; and its weight, on the view that its original form is fiʿāl, is that the hamzah was deleted, giving ʿāl. When we adopt the views mentioned earlier, the alif-lām in it is an inseparable extra; and its deletion is anomalous, as in their saying "Lāha abūka," just as the deletion of the alif in "aqbala sayl" is anomalous. (Aqbala means "came from the presence of Allah.") Some claimed that the alif-lām in Allah is part of the word itself, and the hamzah was joined because of frequent use; this is the view chosen by Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī and al-Suhaylī, but it is wrong, because its weight would then be faʿʿāl, and the absence of tanwīn has no requirement, which indicates that al-  is a letter attached to the word which caused the tanwīn to drop. This name is distinguished by rulings mentioned in the science of grammar. Among the strange things said: its origin is lāhā in Syriac, then it was Arabized, as the poet said:

"Like the oath of Abū Rabāḥ, which his great ones hear."

Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī said: it is non-Arabic, for the Jews and Christians say lāhā, and the Arabs took this word and changed it, saying Allah. Among the strange things said about Allah is that it is an attribute and not a proper name of essence, because the proper name is that by which the named is identified, and Allah, exalted is He, is not perceived by the senses or by immediate knowledge, and His essence is not known by His name, but rather only by His attributes; so making it a name for the essence has no benefit. The knowledge (ʿalam) stands in place of pointing, and pointing is impossible with regard to Allah, exalted is He. The final alif of Allah was deleted so that it would not be confused in the writing of Allāh with the active participle of the verb lahā yalhū (to be heedless). It was also said it was dropped for lightness, and it was also said it is a dialect and was used in writing.

(al-Raḥmān): fa‘lān from raḥmah (mercy). Its pattern originally derives from intensive forms of intransitive verbs, though an anomalous instance from transitive verbs exists. The alif-lām in it is for dominance, as it is in al-ṣaʿq. It is an attribute that has not been used for anyone other than Allah, just as His name has not been used for anyone else. We have heard of His virtues; they say: "Raḥmān of this world and the next." To describe other than Allah with it is part of the obstinacy of the heretics. If you say "Allah is Raḥmān," there are two views on its diptote/triptote status (ṣarf): one is traced to the general principle that the original status of a noun is to take tanwīn (ṣarf), and the other to a specific principle that the original status of the pattern fa‘lān is to be non-declinable (man‘), because of its dominance in this pattern. Among the strange things said about it: it is non-Arabic with the letter khāʾ (kh), then Arabized with ḥāʾ (ḥ), as said by Thaʿlab.

(al-Raḥīm): faʿīl, transformed from fāʿil for intensification; it is one of the five patterns of intensive form: faʿʿāl, faʿūl, mifʿāl, faʿīl and faʿil. Some added fiʿʿīl to them, as in sikkīr. There is a well-known section on it in grammar. It is said that raḥīm also comes in the sense of marḥūm (one who is shown mercy). Al-ʿAmallas ibn ʿAqīl said:

"So when the earth bites you with a bite, you are inclined toward and shown mercy."

ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, Qatādah, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jubayr, Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ḥibbān and Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq said: al-Fātiḥah is Meccan, and this is supported by ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 87]. Surat al-Ḥijr is Meccan by consensus. In the ḥadīth of Ubayy: it is "the seven oft-repeated" and "the seven long surahs," revealed after al-Ḥijr by some time. There is no disagreement that the obligation of prayer was in Mecca, and it is not recorded that there was any prayer in Islam without ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 2]. Abū Hurayrah, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, Mujāhid, Sawād ibn Ziyād, al-Zuhrī and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: it is Medinan. It was also said: it is both Meccan and Medinan.

The bāʾ in bismi Llāh is for seeking help, as in "I wrote with the pen" (katabtu bi-l-qalam); its place is in the accusative (naṣb), meaning "I begin" (bada'tu), and this is the view of the Kufan grammarians. Likewise, every doer who begins his act with the basmalah, its verb is implied as "abdaʾ." Al-Zamakhsharī estimated it to be a verb other than "I began," and placed it later, saying: its estimate is "In the name of Allah I read" or "I recite," since what comes after the basmalah is what is recited; and to front the element before the governing verb, in his view, implies exclusivity; but that is not as he claimed. Sībawayh, while discussing "I struck Zayd," said the following verbatim: "If you front the noun, it is good Arabic, just as that is; i.e., delaying it is good Arabic, which is: Zaydan ḍarabtu." The emphasis and concern here lie in the fronting and delaying, the same as in ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran or ḍaraba Zaydan ʿAmrun. End of quote. It was also said: the place of the noun is in the nominative (raf‘), the estimate being "my beginning is established" or "settled through the name of Allah"; this is the view of the Basran grammarians. Whichever of the two estimates is stronger: the first is preferred, because the original principle is that governing belongs to the verb, or the second for the preservation of one of the two components of the predication.

The noun (ism) is a word that signifies by convention something existing in the perceived world if it is sensible, or in the minds if it is intelligible, without the form itself indicating time. Its signified meaning is the named (musammā). For this reason Sībawayh said: "All is noun, verb and particle." Naming (tasmiyah) is making that word a sign of that meaning. The distinction between the noun, the named and the act of naming is thus clear. When you attribute a judgment to a noun, sometimes the attribution is literal, as in: "Zayd is the name of your son." Sometimes the attribution is possible only figuratively, which is when you use the noun while meaning by it its signified, the named; as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 78], and ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1], and ﴿You worship besides Him only names you have named, you and your fathers﴾ [Yūsuf: 40]. It is remarkable how people differ over whether the noun is identical with the named or other than it; al-Ghazālī, Ibn al-Sayyid, al-Suhaylī and others have written on this, mentioning the arguments of each of the two positions and going into detail. Al-Suhaylī, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1] as meaning that He inserted the word "name" to alert that the meaning is "glorify your Lord and mention your Lord with your heart and tongue," so that the remembrance and glorification are not devoid of utterance by the tongue; because remembrance by the heart has as its object the named, signified by the name, while remembrance by the tongue has as its object the word. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You worship besides Him only names﴾ [Yūsuf: 40], means they are false names, not corresponding to a reality; so it is as if they had worshipped only the names they invented, and this is a striking figurative usage.

The alif is deleted from bism here in the writing for lightness, because of frequent use. If it were written with (the names) al-Qāhir or al-Qādir, al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash said the alif would be deleted; al-Farrāʾ said it is deleted only with ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, because use is frequent only in it; but with other names of Allah, exalted is He, there is no disagreement that the alif remains.

al-Raḥmān is an attribute of Allah according to the majority. Al-Aʿlam and others held that it is a substitute (badal), claiming that al-Raḥmān is a proper name even though it is derived from mercy; but it is not on the level of al-Raḥīm or al-Rāḥim; rather it is like al-Dabarān, which, though derived from dabara, was formed for use as a proper name, and so came on a pattern not found in adjectives. He said: what proves its being a proper name is that it occurs without following a preceding name, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Gracious, established on the Throne﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 5]; ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 1]; ﴿Taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 2]. When proper-nounhood is established, the adjectival role is excluded, so substitution is the only option. Abū Zayd al-Suhaylī said: substitution is impossible in it in my view, and likewise ʿaṭf al-bayān (explicative apposition), because the first noun does not need clarification, since it is the most recognized and clearest of all proper names; do you not see that they said: "And what is al-Raḥmān?" and did not say: "And what is Allah?" So it is an attribute intended to express praise, even though it operates in the manner of proper names.

**[Verse 3]: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.** It is said that the two words have the same meaning, like *nadmān* and *nadīm* (both meaning "companion"). It is also said that their meanings differ: *al-Raḥmān* is more intensive in emphasis, and the expected order would have been ascending, as when one says *ʿālim nirrīr* (a very learned scholar) or *shujāʿ bāsil* (a very brave man). However, *al-Raḥmān*, which encompasses the great blessings and their roots, was followed by *al-Raḥīm* so that it would act as a complement and a follow-up, encompassing what is fine and subtle among them. Al-Zamakhsharī preferred this view. It is also said that *al-Raḥīm* is more intensive. What appears to be correct is that the aspects of intensity differ, which is why the two are combined, and so this is not a case of emphasis (*tawkīd*). The intensive form *faʿlān*, like *ghaḍbān* (very angry) and *sakrān* (very drunk), denotes fullness and dominance, while the intensive form *faʿīl* denotes repetition and reaching the places of mercy. For this reason *faʿlān* is not transitive, whereas *faʿīl* is transitive. One says *Zayd raḥīm al-masākīn* (Zayd is merciful to the needy), just as it takes an object like the active participle. They also said *Zayd ḥafīẓ ʿilmika wa ʿilm ghayrika* (Zayd preserves your knowledge and the knowledge of others), which Ibn Sīdah related from the Arabs.

Whoever holds that the two have one meaning and does not regard one as an emphasis of the other needs to assign each one a specific thing, even though the basic subject matter is considered one, in order to avoid being emphatic. Mujāhid said: *al-Raḥmān* is the mercy of this world and *al-Raḥīm* is the mercy of the Hereafter. Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*al-Raḥmān* is the mercy of this world and *al-Raḥīm* is the mercy of the Hereafter." When this interpretation is authentic, it must be adopted. Al-Qurṭubī said: *Raḥmān* of the Hereafter and *Raḥīm* of this world. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is for the people of the heavens and the earth. ʿIkrimah said: with one mercy and with a hundred mercies. Al-Muzanī said: with the blessing of this world and the religion. Al-ʿAzīzī said: *al-Raḥmān* is toward all His creation, in the rains, the blessings of the senses, and the general blessings; *al-Raḥīm* is toward the believers, in guiding them and being gentle with them. Al-Muḥāsibī said: with the mercy of souls and the mercy of hearts. Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: for the welfare of the Hereafter and of livelihood. Al-Ṣādiq said: the word is particular in form with a general sense regarding provision, and general in form with a particular sense regarding the forgiveness of the believer. Thaʿlab said: *al-Raḥmān* is more praiseworthy and *al-Raḥīm* is gentler. It is also said: *al-Raḥmān* is the Bestower of blessings whose kind cannot be conceived among servants, and *al-Raḥīm* is the Bestower of blessings whose kind can be conceived among servants.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: *al-Raḥmān* is a name general to all kinds of mercy and is specific to Allah, while *al-Raḥīm* pertains only to the believers, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 43].

Attributing mercy to Allah, exalted is He, is a metaphor for His bestowing favor upon His servants. Do you not see that when a king inclines toward his subjects and feels compassion for them, his kindness reaches them, and so mercy in that case is an attribute of action (*ṣifat fiʿl*)? Others said: mercy is the will for good for whomever Allah, exalted is He, wills it for, and in that case it is an attribute of essence (*ṣifat dhāt*). From this disagreement another disagreement follows: are Allah's essential and active attributes eternal, or are the attributes of essence eternal while the attributes of action are originated? There are two opinions. As for the mercy found among servants, it is said that it is a tenderness that arises in the heart. It is also said that it is the intention of good or the averting of harm, because a person may avert harm from one toward whom he feels no tenderness, and may deliver good to one toward whom he feels no tenderness.

Among the rhetorical features of the basmalah are two types. The first is omission (*ḥadhf*), which is what the preposition *bāʾ* in *bismi* depends on, and this has already been mentioned. Omission is said to be for the lightening of the utterance, like their saying *bi-l-rafāʾ wa-l-banīn* (with well-being and children), *bi-l-yumn wa-l-barakah* (with blessing and abundance), and *fa-qultu ilā al-ṭaʿām* (so I said: to the food), and His saying, exalted is He, "among nine signs," meaning *aʿrastu* (I married), *halummū* (come), and *idhhab* (go). Abū al-Qāsim al-Suhaylī said: it is not as they claim, for if that were so, then mentioning it or omitting it would be lightening in every case of omission. Rather, there is a benefit in omitting it: this is a place where nothing should be placed first except the mention of Allah, exalted is He. If the verb were mentioned, and it cannot do without its agent, the mention of Allah would not be placed first. Omitting it creates a correspondence between word and meaning, just as you say in prayer *Allāhu Akbar* (Allah is greatest), whose meaning is "greater than everything," but it is omitted so that the utterance on the tongue corresponds to the intention of the heart, which is that nothing be in the heart except Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Among the omissions is also the omission of the *alif* in *bismi Allāh* and in *al-Raḥmān* in the script, and this is due to frequent use.

The second type is repetition in the description (*takrār fī al-waṣf*), which occurs either to glorify the described subject or for emphasis, so that it becomes firmly fixed in the soul. The exegetes in their books addressed the ruling on saying the basmalah in prayer, mentioned the scholars' disagreement on this, and elaborated extensively on its subsidiary details, and they did likewise in more than one verse. The subject of this belongs in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*). Similarly, some spoke about seeking refuge (*taʿawwudh*) and its ruling, but it is not part of the Qur'an by consensus (*ijmāʿ*). In this book of ours, we do not address a legal ruling unless the wording of the Qur'an indicates that ruling, or it can be deduced from it by one of the methods of deduction.

There is a difference regarding joining *al-Raḥīm* to *al-Ḥamd*. Some Kufan readers recited with a sukun on the *mīm* and paused on it, beginning with a cut hamzah. The majority pronounce the *mīm* with a kasrah and join the *alif* of *al-Ḥamd*. Al-Kisāʾī related from some Arabs that they recite *al-Raḥīm al-Ḥamd* with a fatḥah on the *mīm* and a connected *alif*, as if you had made the *mīm* quiescent and cut the *alif*, then transferred its vowel onto the *mīm* and dropped the *alif*. This reading has not been related as a recitation from anyone.

**"Al-hamd"** is praise for a beautiful quality, whether of a blessing or of something else, expressed by the tongue alone. Its opposite is **dhamm** (dispraise). It is not a metathesis (inverted form) of **madaha** (to praise), contrary to Ibn al-Anbari, since the two are equivalent in their morphological derivations (**tasrifat**, inflectional forms). Praise (**al-madh**) can also attach to inanimate things: one says "you praise a gem" (**tamdahu jawharatan**), but one does not say "you *tahmad* it." **Al-hamd** and **al-shukr** (gratitude) have one meaning. Alternatively, **al-hamd** is more general, while **al-shukr** is praise of God for His acts, and **al-hamd** is praise for His attributes. There are three opinions, the soundest of which is that **al-hamd** is more general. Thus the one who praises (**al-hamid**) is of two kinds: one who thanks (**shakir**) and one who praises by attributes (**muthni bil-sifat**).

**"Lillah"** (to/for God). The **lam** (ل) has the following meanings: possession and the like; transfer of ownership and the like; entitlement; attribution (nisba); causation (ta'lil); conveyance of a message (tabligh); wonder (ta'ajjub); specification (tabyin); becoming (sayrura); the sense of "in," "at," or "after" (zarfiyya); end-point (intiha'); and elevation (isti'la'). Examples: "that wealth is for Zayd" (dhalika al-mal li-Zayd); "I will continue to enjoy for you what you enjoy for me" (adumu laka ma tadumu li); "I gave you a dinar" (wahabtu laka dinaran); ﴿He made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 72]; "the robe is for the girl" (al-jilbab lil-jariya); "Zayd has a paternal uncle" (li-Zayd 'amm); ﴿that you may judge among the people﴾ [al-Nisa: 105]; "I said to you" (qultu laka); "for God, an eye" (lillahi 'aynan, an oath-like usage); "who saw?" (man ra'a); "who excelled?" (man tafawwaqa); ﴿Come, you (it is for you)﴾ [Yusuf: 23]; ﴿that they may become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]; ﴿the just scales for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya: 47]; "it was written for five nights passed" (kutiba li-khams khalawna); ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78]; ﴿We drove it to a dead land﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]; ﴿they fall down upon their chins﴾ [al-Isra: 107].

**"Rabb al-'alamin"** (Lord of the worlds). **Al-Rabb** means the lord, the owner, the one who is established, the one who is worshipped, and the one who sets things right. Some have added the meaning of "companion," citing the poet:

*"The lord of the dogs approached him with his hand, with white (arrows) whose feathers are thin and striped."*

Others take it to mean the Creator who knows, having no singular form, like **al-anam** (cattle). Its derivation is from **al-'ilm** (knowledge) or **al-'alama** (sign). Its referent is every living being, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or humankind, as said by al-Bajali; or humans, jinn and angels, also said by Ibn 'Abbas; or humans, jinn, angels and devils, said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra'; or the two weighty creations (al-thaqalan, humans and jinn), said by Ibn 'Atiyya; or the children of Adam, said by Abu Mu'adh; or the people of Paradise and Hell, said by al-Sadiq; or those who receive provision, said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd; or every created thing, said by al-Hasan and Qatada; or the spiritual beings (al-ruhaniyyun), said by some. Various numbers of "worlds" and their locations have been reported from earlier scholars. God knows the correct view.

Most readers recite the **dal** of **al-hamd** with a **damma** (ḥamdu). Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla made the **mim** of it follow the **lam** of the genitive (**lam al-jarr**) by its **damma** (i.e., **lillahu** with **u**), as al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali made the **kasra** of the **dal** follow the **kasra** of the **lam** (i.e., **hamdi lillahi**). The latter is stranger, because it makes the vowel of an inflected word (**mu'rab**) follow the vowel of a non-inflected position (**ghayr i'rab**), whereas the former is the reverse. In al-Hasan's reading there is the possibility that the following applies to a nominative or accusative word, and in that case the inflection, on both assumptions, is "understood" (**muqaddar**), being prevented from appearing by the word being occupied with the vowel of following (**harakat al-ittiba'**), as in the reported form (**al-mahkiy**) and in the assimilated form (**al-mudgham**). Harun al-'Ataki, Ru'ba and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna read **al-hamda** in the accusative.

**Al-hamd** is a verbal noun (masdar) made definite by **al**. It is either for a known referent (**al-'ahd**), meaning "the praise known among you is for God"; or for defining the essence (**ta'rif al-mahiyya**), as in "the dinar is better than the dirham," meaning whichever dinar it is, is better than whichever dirham it is, which then entails all kinds of praise; or for defining the genus (**ta'rif al-jins**), which indicates by direct denotation (**al-mutabaqa**) the encompassing of all kinds of praise. Originally **al-hamd** is not pluralized, since it is a verbal noun. Ibn al-A'rabi transmitted its plural as **ahmad**, as if its compiler considered the variety of types, and he said:

*"A radiant one, praised in reputation, I have singled him out with the best of my words and the best of my praises."*

The nominative reading is more suitable in meaning, and for this reason all seven readers agreed upon it, because it indicates that praise is established and settled for God, so that He has informed that praise is settled for God, that is, His praise and the praise of others. The meaning of the **lam** in **lillah** is entitlement. Whoever reads it in the accusative must have a governing verb, estimated as "I praise God" (**uhmadu Allah**) or "I praised God" (**hamidtu Allah**); so the praise is specified by the specification of its agent, and it indicates renewal and occurrence. In the accusative case, it is one of the verbal nouns whose verbs have been omitted and which have been put in their place, as in the case of informative (expressive) usage, such as "thanks, not disbelief" (shukran la kufran). Some estimated the governing word for the accusative to be a verb not derived from **al-hamd**, meaning "I say, 'Praise is for God'" (**uqulu al-hamdu lillah**), or "keep to praising God" (**ilzamu al-hamda lillah**), just as they omitted it in such forms as "O God, [give] a hyena and a wolf" (**allahumma dab'an wa dhi'ban**). The first is the correct one, because the utterance indicates it. In the accusative reading, the **lam** indicates specification, as in "I mean God" (**a'ni lillah**), and it is not a strengthening particle for transitivity; so **lillahi** is in the position of an accusative governed by the verbal noun, since the verbal noun cannot govern it. They say "irrigation for Zayd" (**suqyan li-Zayd**), and they do not say "irrigation Zayd" (**suqyan Zaydan**), making it govern it; this shows that it is not an object of the verbal noun, but has become attached to another governing word.

Zayd ibn 'Ali and a group read **Rabba al-'alamin** in the accusative as a praise (**'ala al-madh**). It is eloquent, were it not for the genitive case of the epithets following it, which would then be weak. However, it is reported from Ibn 'Ali's reading that he recited **Rabba al-'alamin al-Rahmana al-Rahim** with all three in the accusative, in which case there is no weakness. The reading of **rabb** in the accusative and the epithets after it in the genitive is weak, because the grammarians stated that there is no following (**itba'**) after a break (**qat'**) in epithets. Nevertheless, its explanation is that **al-Rahman** is a substitute (**badal**), especially according to the view of al-A'lam, who does not permit **al-Rahman** to be an epithet; and for others, it is made acceptable because it is a specific epithet, and because the substitute is on the intention of repeating the governing word, so it is as if it were a new sentence, and hence the accusative is good. The claim of one who asserted that **rabb** is accusative by a verb indicated by the preceding speech, as if it were said, "We praise God, Lord of the worlds," is weak, because it is taking account of an imagined form (**muraa'at al-tawahhum**), which is one of the special features of conjunction (**'atf**), and it is not analogically applicable in it. As for the one who claimed it is accusative as a substitute, it is weak because of the separation by the phrase **al-Rahman al-Rahim**.

**Rabb** is a verbal noun described by it, according to one of the ways of describing by a verbal noun, or it is an active participle (**ism fa'il**) whose alif has been dropped, so its origin is **rabb** (from **rabb**, the active form meaning one who nurtures), as they say **rajul barr** and **barr** (a dutiful man). They applied the word **al-Rabb** to God alone; for others it is restricted by an annexation (**idafa**), as in **rabb al-dar** (master of the house).

The **al** in **al-'alamin** is for totality (**al-istighraq**). The plural of **al-'alam** is irregular, since it is a collective noun (**ism jam'**), and its plural with the sound masculine suffix (**al-waw wal-nun**) is even more irregular, because it fails to meet some of the conditions of this plural form. What I prefer is that it applies to those who are morally responsible (**al-mukallafin**), based on His saying, ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those of knowledge﴾ [al-Rum: 22]; and the reading of Hafs with a **kasra** on the **lam** clarifies this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 1, verse 3:

﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Discussion of these two was already given under the basmala. Together with His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2], they are attributes of praise (sifat madh), because what precedes them is a proper name (alam) that, in the basmala, has no shared sense requiring specification. He began with the attribute of lordship (ar-rububiyya). If al-Rabb (the Lord) means the master (al-sayyid), or the owner (al-malik), or the one worshipped (al-ma'bud), then it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l) for the one so described, since He disposes of the one who is mastered, the one who is owned, and the worshipper as He wills, with good and with evil. This calls for the attributes of ar-Rahmaniyya and ar-Rahimiyya, so that the servant's hope for pardon expands if he slips, and his hope grows stronger if he falters. It is not sound for al-Rabb to mean "the one who is constant" (al-thabit) or "the companion" (al-sahib), because it cannot be attached to ﴿the worlds﴾. If it means "the one who sets things right" (al-muslih), then the attribute of mercy suggests few corrections, because what moves a person to set right the condition of another is his mercy toward him.

The meaning of the sentence and of the attributes is that whoever is described with lordship and with mercy toward those who are lorded over deserves praise.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ar-Rahmani ar-Rahimi﴾ in the genitive (khafd). Abu al-Aliya, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and Isa ibn Amr read them in the accusative (nasb). Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Rabi ibn Khaytham, and Abu Imran al-Juni read them in the nominative (raf'). The genitive is by way of qualification (na't). It has also been said that the genitive is a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition (atf bayan), and some of this has already been mentioned. The accusative and nominative are by way of change of case (qat') for emphasis.

As for the repetition of ﴿ar-Rahmani ar-Rahimi﴾: if the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha, the repetition draws attention to the great worth of these two attributes and to the emphasis on their importance. Makki (Makki ibn Abi Talib) took their repetition as evidence that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha. He said: if it were a verse, we would have two adjacent verses with one meaning, and that does not occur except with intervening elements separating the first from the second. He said: the separation between them by ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2] is no separation at all, because it is postponed while what is meant is precedence. Its estimated order is: "Praise be to God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, Lord of the worlds." We say it is precedence because the juxtaposition of mercy with praise is more fitting, and the juxtaposition of sovereignty with kingship is more fitting. He said: (p-20) Precedence and postposition are common in the Qur'an, and Makki's statement is flawed in more than one respect. Were it not for the eminence of its speaker, I would have kept my book free of mentioning it. The Qur'anic arrangement is in the utmost eloquence, because He, may He be exalted, described Himself with the attribute of lordship and the attribute of mercy, then mentioned two things: one of them is His ownership of the Day of Recompense, and the second is worship. Sovereignty suits lordship, and worship suits mercy. So the first corresponds to the first, and the second to the second.

The exegetes have mentioned pausing (al-waqf) in the science of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), and its divisions have been disputed. It has been said that there are the complete pause (tamm), the sufficient pause (kafi), the ugly pause (qabih), and other kinds. People have written books on this arranged by surah, such as the book of Abu Amr al-Dani, the book of al-Kirmani, and others. Whoever has a share of the science of Arabic (ilm al-arabiyya) can do without that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 1, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Māliki﴾: Ṣāʾim, Ṣaʿaba... *(see note below)*

Let me correct that opening line and provide the full translation:

﴿Māliki﴾ (Master of): ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read *Māliki* in the form *fāʿil* with a *kasra* (*bil-khafḍ*), and Khalaf in his own choice of reading, and Yaʿqūb. This is the reading of the ten (qurrāʾ), except Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr. It was also the reading of many of the Companions, among them Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd, Muʿādh and Ibn ʿAbbās, and of the Successors, among them Qatāda and al-Aʿmash.

The rest of the seven read *Malik* in the form *faʿil* with a *kasra*, as did Zayd, Abū al-Dardāʾ, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Miswar, and many of the Companions and Successors.

*Malk* in the form *saháh* was read by Abū Hurayra, ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī, and it was transmitted by al-Juʿfī and ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr. This is the dialect of Bakr ibn Wāʾil.

*Malikī* with the *kasra* of the *kāf* prolonged was read by Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ, from Warsh, from Nāfiʿ.

*Milk* in the form *ʿijl* was read by Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, al-Shaʿbī and ʿAṭiyya, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributed it to Abū Ḥayāt.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: Anas ibn Mālik and Abū Nawfal ʿUmar ibn Muslim ibn Abī ʿAdī read *Malika Yawm al-Dīn* with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* and without an *alif*. This also came from Abū Ḥayāt. End of quote.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿĀʾisha and Muwriq al-ʿIjlī read it the same way, except that they raised the *kāf*.

*Malaka* as a past-tense verb was read by Abū Ḥayāt, Abū Ḥanīfa, Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, Abū ʿĀṣim ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī, and Abū al-Maḥshar ʿĀṣim ibn Maymūn al-Jaḥdarī, so that they put the *yawm* in the accusative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned that this is the reading of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

*Mālika* with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* was read by al-Aʿmash, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, ʿUthmān ibn Abī Sulaymān and ʿAbd al-Malik, judge of India. Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned that it is the reading of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān and Abū ʿAbd al-Malik al-Shāmī.

Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim transmitted from al-Yamān *malikan* with a *fatḥa* and *tanwīn*.

*Mālikun* with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf* and *tanwīn* was read by ʿAwn al-ʿUqaylī. It was also transmitted from Khalaf ibn Hishām, Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim, with the *yawm* in the accusative.

*Māliku Yawmi* with a *ḍamma* and an idāfa was read by Abū Hurayra, Abū Ḥayāt and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz in one of the two reports from him. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ attributed it to Abū Rawḥ ʿAwn ibn Abī Shaddād al-ʿUqaylī, resident of Basra.

*Malīki* in the form *faʿīl* was read by Ubayy, Abū Hurayra and Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī.

*Mālik* with a strong *imāla* (vowel-inclination) was read by Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, and an intermediate *imāla* by Qutayba ibn Mihrān from al-Kisāʾī. 

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī was ignorant of the transmission concerning the *imāla* reading. He said: No one among the reciters gave an *imāla* to the *alif* of *Mālik*. That is permissible, but one does not recite by what is merely permissible unless there is a widely-transmitted report for it. He also mentioned that in the irregular (shādhdh) readings it was read *Mallāk*, with an *alif*, a *shadda* on the *lām*, and a *kasra* on the *kāf*.

So these are thirteen readings. Some of them go back to *al-Malk* and some to *al-Milk*. The lexicographers said: Both go back to *al-Malk*, which means "binding," and from it comes *malk al-ʿajīn* (kneading the dough).

Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm said:
*"I held it with my hand, and I tore open its seam; the one standing from beyond it sees what is behind it."*

*Al-Imlāk* means tying the knot of marriage. One of the fine points of this root is that all six of its permutations are used in the language, and all of them go back to the meaning of strength and firmness, so there is a common core among them all. This is called *ishtiqāq al-akbar* (the "greater derivation"). No one went to this view except Abū al-Fatḥ (Ibn Jinnī). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī would be comfortable with it in some places. These permutations are: *malaka, makala, kamkala, lakama, kamula, kalama*.

Al-Fakhr al-Rāzī claimed that the permutation *kamkala* is unused, and that is not correct. Rather, it is used, as evidenced by what al-Farrāʾ cited from the words of the poet:
*"When he saw that I had made his departure difficult, he took hold, though taking hold would not benefit him."*

*Al-Mulk* is subjugation and control over one who can be obeyed, and this may be by right or without right. *Al-Malk* is subjugation over one who can be obeyed and over one who cannot, and this from him is by right. So between them there is a general and specific relation from one aspect.

Al-Akhfash said: It is said *malaka* from *al-mulk* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*, and *mālik* from *al-milk* with a *kasra* or *fatḥa* on the *mīm*. They claimed that a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* is a dialect for this meaning.

It was transmitted from some Baghdadis: *Lī fī hādhā al-wādī mulkun wa milkun bi-maʿnan wāḥid* ("In this valley I have *mulk* and *milk* with one meaning").

﴿Yawmi﴾: *al-Yawm* is the period from the rising of dawn to the setting of the sun, and it is also applied to any period of time. Its structure is unusual, meaning the existence of a root in which the first radical is *yāʾ* and the middle radical is *wāw*. Nothing of this pattern came except *yawm* and its inflections. *Yūḥ* is a name for the sun, and some claimed that it is *būj* with a *bāʾ* and a dotted letter with one dot from below.

﴿al-Dīn﴾: *al-Jazāʾ* (recompense): "He repaid them as they had done," said by Qatāda. *Al-Ḥisāb* (reckoning): ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ [al-Tawba: 36], said by Ibn ʿAbbās. *Al-Qaḍāʾ* (judgment): ﴿and let not compassion for them seize you in the religion of God﴾ [al-Nūr: 2]. *Al-Ṭāʿa* (obedience): "the religion of ʿAmr," and "Fadak came between us and you," said by Abū al-Faḍl. *Al-ʿĀda* (custom): "like your *dīn* from Umm al-Ḥuwayrith before her," and he meant by it here the action, said by al-Farrāʾ. *Al-Milla* (creed): ﴿And I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ [al-Māʾida: 3], ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19]. *Al-Qahr* (domination), and from it *al-madīn* for the slave and *al-madīna* for the community, said by Yamān ibn Riʾāb.

Abū ʿAmr al-Zāhid said: "Even if he obeyed or disobeyed, humbled or exalted, subdued or oppressed, and ruled."

The people of lexicography reported: *Dintuhu bi-fiʿlihi daynan* with a *fatḥa* or *kasra* on the *dāl* means "I repaid him for his deed."

It is said: *al-Dayn* is the verbal noun, and *al-Dīn* with a *kasra* is the noun. *Al-Dīn* also means politics, and *al-Dayyān* means the one who governs. Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ said about it: *"Nor are you my governor so that you could rebuke me."*

*Al-Dīn* also means condition. Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "I asked a Bedouin about something, and he said: If you had met me on a religion other than this, I would have informed you." 

*Al-Dīn* also means illness, from al-Liḥyānī, and he cited:
*"O illness of your heart from Salmā, and it has become ill."*

Whoever read the *kāf* with a *kasra* (*Māliki*) understood it as an adjective. If it is in the form of *milk* on the pattern *fiʿl* with a *kasra* or sukūn on the ʿayn, or *malīk* with the same meaning, then it is clear, because it describes a definite noun with a definite noun. If it is in the form *mālik*, *mallāk* or *malīk* transformed from *mālik* for intensity, it is definite too. This is supported by the reading of the one who read *malaka yawma al-dīn* as a past-tense verb. If it has the meaning of the future, which is the apparent meaning, because the Day has not yet come, then it is problematic. This is because when the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) has the meaning of the present or future, its *idāfa* is not pure (*ghayr maḥḍa*), so it does not become definite by the *idāfa*. If it is annexed to a definite noun, it cannot then be an adjective, because a definite noun is not described by an indefinite one, and an indefinite noun is not a *badal* (substitute) for a definite one, because substitution by adjectives is weak.

The resolution of this problem: if the active participle has the meaning of the present or future, two possibilities are allowed. The first is what we mentioned earlier: it does not become definite by what is annexed to it, since it is intended to be separated from the *idāfa*, and because it governs the accusative verbally. The second is that it becomes definite by it when it is definite, so that the described noun becomes known by this description, and its restriction by time is not considered. This second view is rare in transmission, and no one knows it except one who has knowledge of the book of Sībawayh and has searched for its subtleties.

Sībawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: "Yūnus and al-Khalīl claimed that the annexed adjectives which become adjectives of an indefinite noun may all be definite, and this is known in the speech of the Arabs." End of quote. He made an exception from this, which is only the category of the *ṣifa mushabbaha* (resembling adjective), which does not become definite by *idāfa*, such as *ḥasan al-wajh* ("beautiful of face").

Whoever raised the *kāf* and gave it *tanwīn* or did not give it *tanwīn*, then it is by cutting it to the nominative. Whoever put it in the accusative, then it is by cutting it to the accusative, or as a vocative. Cutting is rarer because of the harmony of the descriptions, since it does not leave them by cutting.

Whoever read *malaka* as a past-tense verb, then it is a declarative clause with no place in the grammatical structure (*lā mawḍiʿa lahā min al-iʿrāb*).

Whoever prolonged the *kasra* of the *kāf* read a rare reading, or what is mentioned as impermissible except in poetry.

The *idāfa* of *al-milk* or *al-mulk* to *yawm al-dīn* is only from the category of expansion (*ittisāʿ*), since their object is other than the Day, and the *idāfa* is with the meaning of *lām* and not with the meaning of *fī*, against those who established the *idāfa* with the meaning of *fī*. The explanation of this is discussed in grammar. (p-22) If it is from *al-milk*, it is from the pattern of:
*"The cook of the hours of sleep, sloth has increased."*

The apparent meaning of the language is that *malik* and *mālik* differ, as was mentioned earlier. It is said that both have one meaning, like *farih* and *fārih* (both meaning "exultant" or "strong"). If we say they differ, then it is said *mālik* is more praiseworthy because its *idāfa* is good to what the *malik* cannot be annexed to, like *mālik al-jinn wa al-insi wa al-malāʾika wa al-ṭayr* ("Master of jinn, humans, angels and birds"). So it is broader in including rational beings and others. The poet said:
*"Glory be to Him, to whose Face the faces are humbled, King of kings and Master of the dust."*

Al-Akhfash said: It is not said here *milk*, and in their saying *mālik al-shayʾ* it applies to one who owns it, and one may be a *malik* without being a *mālik*, like *milk al-ʿArab wa al-ʿAjam*, as Abū Ḥātim said. And because of its addition in the structure, and the Arabs magnify by addition in the structure. And because of the addition in the parts of the second, since it adds letters. And because of the number of those who read it. And because it allows disposal by sale, gift and transfer of ownership. And to keep ownership in the hand of the owner if he acts with injustice, transgression or extravagance. And because it is specified for the Day of Resurrection. And because kings cannot seize it from the king. And because of the great hope placed in the Lord by seeking what one needs, and because of the obligation to serve Him. And because the owner hopes for it, while the king hopes for you. And because He has mercy and compassion, while the king has awe and governance.

It is also said: *malik* is more praiseworthy and more fitting if it is not described of God, Exalted is He, because it signifies multiplicity, and because it praises by "Owner of the kingdom," and it did not say "Owner of the kingdom" (*mālik al-mulk*). And so that it agrees with the beginning and the ending in His saying ﴿King of mankind﴾ [al-Nās: 2]. The ending is only with the most noble names. And because the owner comes under the authority of the king. And because He described Himself with kingship in several places. And because of the generality of His disposal over what His kingdom contains, and the restriction of kingship to His possession. This was said by Abū ʿUbayda. And because the king does not need an *idāfa*, or the owner must be annexed to something owned, but the king is greater than people, so he is more noble than the owner.

Abū ʿAlī said: Ibn al-Sarrāj related from one who chose the reading *malik kull shayʾ* by His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 2], so the reading *mālik* is a confirmation. Abū ʿAlī said: There is no proof in this, because in the revelation the general was mentioned first, then the specific part of it was mentioned: ﴿The Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 24]. So *al-Khāliq* is general, and *al-Muṣawwir* was mentioned for what it contains of alerting to the craftsmanship and the aspects of wisdom. From this also: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqara: 4] after His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqara: 3]. He repeated it only to magnify it, and to alert to the obligation of believing in it, and to refute the disbelieving atheists. From this also: *al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm*: mentioning *al-Raḥmān*, which is general, and mentioning *al-Raḥīm* after it to specify mercy for the believers in His saying ﴿and He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 43]. End of quote.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Also, the word *rabb* is used in the speech of the Arabs with the meaning of *milk* (ownership), as in His saying (the poet):
*"And before this you raised me, so the ruler of [the tribe] was ..."*

and the proof is reversed against those who read "malaka." The day to which "malik" or "malik" is added is meant as a period of time extending until the reckoning is over and the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire settle in their abodes. The object of the genitive (al-mudaf ilayh) is in reality the matter (al-amr), as if he said: "Master (malik) or King (malik) of the affair on the Day of Religion." But since the day is a time-frame (zarf) for the affair, it is permissible to extend it so that the king or master governs it, because taking control of the container is taking control of what is contained.

The purpose of specifying this idiomatic addition, although God, exalted is He, is the owner of all times and places, and of whoever dwells in them, and dominion belongs to Him in them, is to draw attention to the greatness of this day because of the great matters and mighty terrors that occur in it: their standing before God, exalted is He, their seeking intercession to hasten the reckoning, the separation between the good-doer and the wrongdoer, and their settling in what God, exalted is He, has promised them both. Or it is (meant to indicate) that it is a day on which everything that He granted to His servants and entrusted to them is returned to God, and on which the ownership of every owner ceases. God, exalted is He, said: "And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone" [Maryam: 95], and "Indeed you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time" [al-An'am: 94].

Ibn al-Sarraj said: The meaning of "Master of the Day of Religion" is that He owns its coming and its occurrence. So the addition to "the day," according to his view, is an addition to the object in reality, not to a time-frame that was extended. The meanings given for "al-din" can all be used with the day as an addition, in the sense of each of them, except "al-millah" (religion as a community of belief).

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and others said: The Day of Religion is the Day of Recompense for deeds and of reckoning. Abu 'Ali said: What supports this is "Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned" [Ghafir: 17], and "Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do" [al-Jathiyah: 28].

Mujahid said: The Day of Religion is the Day of Reckoning, when people are "madinin" (held to account, mu'asabin). In "Master of the Day of Religion" there is evidence for the affirmation of the return (al-ma'ad), the resurrection (al-hashr) and the reckoning (al-hisab). Since God, exalted is He, is described by mercy, the servant becomes expansive and hope prevails over him; so the description of Him as King or Master draws attention, so that his deeds are carried out in awe, and that for his deeds there is a day on which their fruit appears to him, of good and of evil.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 1, verse 5:

﴿Iyyaka﴾ *iyya* is the form to which the attached pronoun suffixes are joined: the *ya'* of the speaker, the *kaf* of the addressee, and the *ha'* of the absent party, along with their variants. It is therefore a detached accusative pronoun, not a noun with an attached pronoun in the genitive, contrary to the claim of the one who holds that view. Is the pronoun *together with* its suffixes, or is the pronoun alone, with the suffixes being particles? Or is it *iyya* together with the suffixes, as nouns to which it is added? Or are the suffixes alone, with *iyya* being an extra element so that the pronouns can be attached to it? These are opinions mentioned in the grammatical literature. As for its dialect forms: with a kasra on the hamza and a shadda on the ya', it is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur), and in this form they recited it; with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the ya', al-Fadl al-Raqashi recited it; with a kasra on the hamza and a light ya' (without shadda), ʿAmr ibn Fa'id recited it, on the authority of Ubayy; with the hamza of the kasra replaced by a ha', and with the hamza of the fatha replaced by a ha', Ibn al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi recited it. Abu ʿUbayda's view that *iyya* is derived (*mushtaqq*) is weak, and Abu ʿUbayda did not have a good command of grammar, although he was a leading authority in the lexicon and in the days (histories) of the Arabs. If it is said that it is derived, its derivation is from the word *āwi* in the saying of the poet:

*So yearn (fa-āwi) for her memory whenever you remember her*

Then it would be of the pattern *quwwa* (a form from the root *ʾ-w-y*). Or it is derived from *al-Aya* (the root with ya' as its middle radical), so its middle letter is a ya', as in the saying of the poet:

*This age has left nothing of his (iyyāʾihi)*

There are two opinions. As for its measure (wazn): is it *af'al*, with the original form *iʾawwa* or *iʾawā*? Or *fa'il*, with the original form *iwyaw* or *iwyay*? Or *fa'ul*, with the original form *iwwaw* or *iwyā*? Or *fa'la*, with the original form *awwā* or *awyā*? All these opinions are weak. The discussion of its inflected forms (*tasarif*) has been so extensive that *iyya* is now mentioned in the science of grammar. The addition of *iyya* to an explicit noun is rare, as in the phrase *wa-iyya al-shawābb* (and [the likes of] the young women), or it is a case of poetic necessity, as in *da'nī wa-iyya Khālid* (leave me and Khalid). Its use in the sense of warning (*tahdhīr*) is well known, so it carries a nominative pronoun, which may be followed by the nominative, as in *iyyāka anta nafsaka* (you yourself, beware of yourself).

﴿Na'budu﴾ *al-ʿibāda* (worship) means submission (*al-tadhallul*), as the majority said; or it means devotion (*al-tajrīd*), as Ibn al-Sikkit said. Its transitivity with the doubled form (*ʿabbada*) differs from its transitivity with the single form (*ʿabada*): *ʿabbadtu al-rajul* means I made the man submissive (*dhallaltuhu*), while *ʿabadtu Allah* means I submitted to God (*dhalaltu lahu*). Al-Hasan, Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited *iyyāka yuʿbadu* with a ya' and in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ūl*). On the authority of some people of Mecca, *naʿbud* is recited with the *dal* sukūn. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Yahya ibn Waththab and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythi recited *naʿbudu* with a kasra on the nun.

﴿Nasta'in﴾ *al-istiʿāna* means seeking help (*ṭalab al-ʿawn*). Seeking (*al-ṭalab*) is one of the meanings of the form *istaf'ala*, and it has twelve meanings: seeking; becoming (*ittihād*, unity or identity); transformation (*taḥawwul*); attributing to something the meaning of what is derived from it, and counting it as such; being the intransitive counterpart (*muṭāwaʿa*) of *af'ala* and corresponding to it; corresponding to *tafaʿʿala* and *iftaʿala* and to the bare verb (*al-fiʿl al-mujarrad*); being sufficient without it and without *fa'ala*, as in *istaṭʿama* (asked for food), *istaʿbadahu* (enslaved him), *istanṣara* (became a Christian), *istaʿẓamahu* (considered him great), and *istaḥsanahu* (found him beautiful), even though it is not used in that way; *istashlā* is the intransitive counterpart of *ashlā*; *istaballa* corresponds to and is the intransitive counterpart of *aballa*; *istakbara* corresponds to *takabbara*; *istaʿṣama* corresponds to *iʿtaṣama*; *istaghnā* corresponds to *ghinā*; *istankafa* and *istaḥyā* are sufficient without the bare verb; and *istarjaʿa* and *istaʿāna* (in the sense of shaving the pubic hair) are sufficient without *fa'ala*. Thus *istaʿāna* means seeking help, like *istaghfara* (sought forgiveness) and *istaʿẓama*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: "It has also come in the form *wiyyāka*, with the hamza replaced by a waw. I do not know whether this is from al-Farra' or from the Arabs." This is the reverse of what they did in words like *ashāḥa* (he dispersed) according to those who pronounce the hamza, because they fled from the kasra on the waw toward the hamza, finding the kasra on the waw burdensome. In *wiyyāka* they fled from the hamza toward the waw. According to the dialect of those who find the hamza burdensome, it is a whole group, because it resembles retching (*al-tahawwuʿ*). The form *istafʿala* also corresponds to *tafāʿala* and *faʿala*. Abu al-Hasan ibn Sidah reported in *al-Muḥkam*: "I held onto the thing (*tamāsaktu bil-shayʾ*), I grasped it (*masaktu bihi*), and I held onto it (*istamsaktu bihi*), with one meaning, that is, I detained myself by it." He said: "One says *masaktu bil-shayʾ*, *amsaktu*, and *tamassaktu*, meaning I held back." End of quotation. Thus the meanings of *istafʿala* become fourteen, by the addition of correspondence to *tafāʿala* and *tafaʿʿala*.

The majority recited the nun of *nastaʿīn* with a fatha; it is the dialect of the Hijaz and it is the eloquent form (*al-fuṣḥā*). ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythi, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Yahya ibn Waththab, al-Nakhaʿi and al-Aʿmash recited it with a kasra. This is the dialect of Qays, Tamim, Asad and Rabiʿa, and the same rule applies to the prefix letter of the present tense in this verb and what resembles it. Abu Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī said: "It is the dialect of Hudhayl." The waw changes to an alif in *istaʿāna* and *mustaʿān*, and to a ya' in *nastaʿīn* and *mustaʿīn*. The deletion in *al-istiʿāna* is mentioned in the science of morphology (*taṣrīf*). *Istaʿāna* is transitive by itself and by means of the preposition *bi-*.

﴿Iyyāka﴾ is a fronted object (*mafʿūl muqaddam*). Al-Zamakhshari claims that it is not fronted before the verb except for restriction (*lil-takhṣīṣ*), so it is as if he said: "We worship none but You." The refutation of his view has already been given in his interpretation of *bismillāh atluwu*, and we have mentioned the text of Sibawayh there. Therefore, in our view, the fronting is only for attention and concern with the object. A Bedouin cursed another Bedouin, who turned away from him and said: "*Iyyāka aʿnī*" (It is you I mean). The other said to him: "*Wa-ʿanka uʿriḍu*" (And it is from you that I turn away). They put the more important first.

*Iyyāka* involves *iltifāt* (a shift in grammatical person, from one person to another in the same discourse), because it is a transition from the third person (absence), since if it followed one uniform pattern it would have been *iyyāhu*. Shifting is one of the techniques of eloquence (*funūn al-balāgha*). It is a shift from absence to address or speech, from address to absence or speech, and from speech to absence or address. Absence may be expressed by an explicit noun or by a pronoun, and its condition is that the referent be one. Do you not see that the one addressed by *iyyāka* is God, exalted is He? They said: the purpose of this *iltifāt* is to display mastery of speech and the ability to handle it freely. Some have mentioned something beyond this: displaying a benefit specific to each place. We will speak about this where something of it occurs to us. Its benefit in *iyyāka naʿbud* is that when he mentioned that praise belongs to God, who is characterized by lordship, mercy, kingship, and the King of the Day mentioned, the praiser turned to inform, as a result of mentioning the praise that is established for Him from Himself and from others, that He and others worship Him and submit to Him. Likewise, he used the *nun* which applies to Him and to others. Just as praise encompasses the praisers, so worship encompasses the speaker and others. A parallel to this is that you mention a person characterized by noble qualities, speaking of him in the manner of an absent party, while that person is present with you, so you say to him: "*Iyyāka aqṣid*" (It is you I intend). In this address there is a gentleness in reaching the desired aim that is not present in the phrase *iyyāhu*. And because he mentioned this as a preparation for the supplication in his saying *ihdinā* (guide us). As for the one who holds that *Malik* is a vocative noun, then *iyyāka* is not an *iltifāt*, because it is an address after an address, although after the vocative it is permissible to use the third person, as the poet said:

*O abode of Mayya at al-ʿAlyāʾ and al-Sanad,*
*it has become desolate, and the ancient eons have passed over it.*

And address after the vocative:

*Ah, O abode of Mayy, be safe amid decay,*
*and may the rain never cease to pour upon your sands.*

The claim of al-Zamakhshari that the three verses of Imru' al-Qays contain three *iltifāt*s is not correct; rather they are two *iltifāt*s:

The first: a departure from the address with which it begins in his saying:

*Your night has grown long with antimony,*
*and the sleepless one has slept, but you have not.*

to the third person in his saying:

*He spent the night, and a night was his,*
*like the night of the one with the sore eye.*

The second: a departure from this third person to speech in his saying:

*And that is from a news that came to me,*
*and I informed him about Abu al-Aswad.*

The interpretation of his words is that the claim of three is an error. As for specifying that the first is the transition from absence to presence, that is a greater error, because this *iltifāt* is one of the accidents of wording, not of the semantic assumptions. Assuming *qūlū* (say) before *al-ḥamdu lillāh*, and also assuming it before *iyyāka*, does not allow an *iltifāt* together with it, and this is a weak view. The scholars of the science of rhetorical ornament (*ʿilm al-badīʿ*) have established a chapter on *iltifāt* in their speech, and Ibn al-Athir al-Jazari spoke about it at length, may God have mercy on him.

The reading of the one who recited *iyyāka yuʿbadu* with a ya' in the passive is problematic, because *iyyāka* is an accusative pronoun and there is no governing verb for it. Its justification is that it contains a metaphor (*istiʿāra*) and an *iltifāt*. The metaphor is placing the accusative pronoun in the position of the nominative pronoun, as if he had said *anta* (you), then he turned and reported about Him in the manner of the absent party, since *iyyāka*, in meaning, is the absent one, so he said *yuʿbadu*. The strangeness of this *iltifāt* is that it occurs within a single sentence. He had in mind the poet's saying:

*Are you the Hilali who once*
*we heard of, and the Arhabi, the conqueror?*

And the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

*Alas for my soul, that the youth of Khalid*
*and the whiteness of your face were for the dusty ground!*

The worship in *iyyāka naʿbud* has been interpreted as submission and humility, which is the original meaning in the lexicon, or obedience, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ [Maryam: 44]; or drawing near through obedience, or supplication, as in ﴿Those who disdain My worship﴾ [Ghafir: 60], meaning My supplication; or monotheism, as in ﴿except that they worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], meaning that they affirm My oneness. All of these are close in meaning. *Istiʿāna* is paired with worship to combine what the servant draws near to God by and what he seeks from Him. Worship is placed before seeking help to put the means first before the request, so that the answer may be attained. Worship and seeking help are stated without qualification so that they may include every object of worship and everything one seeks help against. *Iyyāka* is repeated so that each of worship and seeking help is stated in its own clause, and each is intended. It also serves to explicitly specify seeking help from Him, unlike if it had been *iyyāka naʿbud wa-nastaʿīn*, which could have been understood as a report about seeking help, meaning: and that he seek help, without specifying from whom he seeks it.

Various restrictions have been reported from those affiliated with righteousness regarding worship and seeking help. Some said: "*Iyyāka naʿbud*" means with knowledge, and "*iyyāka nastaʿīn*" means seeking help in it through insight. But there is nothing in the wording that indicates this. In *naʿbud* they said it is a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists), and in *nastaʿīn* a refutation of the Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will). The station of worship is noble, and the command to it came in many places. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And worship your Lord﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]; ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 21]. And it is a metonymy for the most noble of creatures (ﷺ). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1]; ﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. And God, exalted is He, related about Jesus, upon our prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and peace: ﴿He said, "Indeed I am a servant of God"﴾ [Maryam: 30]. God, exalted and sanctified is He, said: ﴿There is no god but Me, so worship Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. He mentioned worship immediately after monotheism, because monotheism is the root and worship is its branch. They said that his saying *iyyāka* is a refutation of the Dahriyya (materialists), the Mu'attila (those who deny divine attributes), and those who deny the existence of the Creator, because it is an address to a present existing being.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 1, verses 6–7 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿Guide us﴾. *Al-hidaya* (guidance) means direction, indication, and going ahead. From it comes *al-hawadi* (the leading animals of a caravan). It also means clarification, as in ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. It may also mean inspiration, as in ﴿He gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50]. The exegetes said its meaning is that He inspired all animals toward their benefits. It may also mean calling, as in ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], meaning a caller. The basic form of *hada* is that it reaches its second object with *li* (to), as in ﴿He guides to what is most upright﴾ [al-Isra: 9], or with *ila* (to), as in ﴿You guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Then its usage widens so that it takes the object directly, as in ﴿Guide us to the path﴾. *Na* is the pronoun of the speaker when accompanied by others, or of the speaker's own self in the majestic sense. It can occupy the position of nominative, accusative, or genitive.

﴿The path﴾: *al-tariq* (the road). Its original form is with *sin*, from *al-sarth*, which means swallowing. From this the road was called *laqm* (a swallowing). Qunbul and Ruways recited it with *sin*, in accordance with the original form. Replacing its *sin* with *sad* is the most eloquent form, the dialect of Quraysh, and the majority recited it this way. It is also how it was written in the *Imam* (the standard codex). Pronouncing it as *zay* is a dialect transmitted by al-Asma'i from Abu Amr. Pronouncing it with *ishmam* (a slight hint of *zay*) is the dialect of Qays, and Hamza recited it this way with variations and detailed differences among his transmitters. Abu Ya'la said: It is transmitted from Abu Amr also: *sin*, *sad*, and *al-mudari'a* (a blend) between *zay* and *sad*. It was transmitted from him by al-Uryan from Abu Sufyan. Al-Asma'i transmitted from Abu Amr that he recited it with a pure *zay*. Some linguists said: What al-Asma'i reported in this recitation is an error on his part. He only heard Abu Amr recite it with *al-mudari'a* and mistook it for *zay*. Al-Asma'i was not a grammarian, so he cannot be trusted in this. Abu Ali related this statement from Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid. Abu Ja'far al-Tusi said in his exegesis, and he is one of the imams of the Imamiyya: *Al-sirat* with *sad* is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is the good dialect. Most Arabs make it *sin*. *Zay* is the dialect of Udhra, Ka'b, and Bani al-Qayn. Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid said: This recitation indicates that the recitation of one who recites between *zay* and *sad* is an effort to produce a letter between two letters, which is difficult on the tongue, and it is not a letter upon which speech is built, nor is it one of the letters of the alphabet. I do not deny that it is from the speech of eloquent Arabs, but *sad* is more eloquent and more widespread. It is used as both masculine and feminine, and its masculine use is more common. Abu Ja'far al-Tusi said: The people of the Hijaz use *al-sirat* as feminine, like *al-tariq*, *al-sabil*, *al-zuqaq*, and *al-suq*. The Banu Tamim use all of these as masculine. In the plural of abundance it is *surut*, like *kitab* and *kutub*. In the plural of paucity its analogical form is *asrita*, like *himar* and *ahmira*. This is when *al-sirat* is masculine. When it is feminine, its analogical form is *af'ul*, like *dhira'* and *adhru'*, and *shimal* and *ashmul*. Zayd ibn Ali, al-Dahhak, and Nasr ibn Ali, from al-Hasan, recited: *Ihdina sirat-an mustaqim-an* (Guide us to a straight path), with tanwin (nunation) and without the definite article, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], ﴿the path of Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 53].

﴿Straight﴾: *istaqama* is *istaf'ala* in the sense of the bare verb without augmentation. This is one of the meanings of *istaf'ala*: that it has the sense of the bare verb, which is *qama*. *Al-qiyam* is standing upright and being level, without crookedness.

* *

﴿The path of those﴾: *alladhina* is a relative pronoun. The more eloquent form is with *ya* in all its three cases. Some Arabs make it with *waw* in the nominative case. Using it with the *nun* dropped is permissible. Some restricted this to poetic necessity, but if it is not for restriction, it is permissible in other cases. The dropping of the *alif-lam* from it has been heard, and they say *alladhina*. The matter of how it is defined is a disputed point discussed in grammar. *Alladhina* is specific to rational beings, unlike *alladhi*, which applies to one who has knowledge and to other things.

﴿You have blessed﴾: *al-ni'ma* is ease and softness of life. For this reason the south wind is called *al-nu'ma* because of the softness of its blowing, and the ostrich is called *al-na'ama* because of the softness of its arrow. *Ni'ma* means one who is in blessing. *An'amtu 'aynahu* means I gladdened his eye. *An'ama 'alayhi* means he exceeded in favoring him. The *hamza* in *an'ama* is for making the thing possessor of what is derived from it, but it has been given the meaning of bestowing favor, so it takes *'ala* (upon). Its original usage is transitive without a preposition: *an'amtuhu*, meaning I made him a possessor of blessing. This is one of the meanings of *af'ala*, which has twenty-four meanings. This is one of them. The others are: transitivity, multiplicity, becoming, assistance, exposure, negation, attaining the thing in the sense of what is derived from it, reaching a number, time, or place, agreeing with the triliteral form, sufficiency from it, reciprocity of one verb with another, attacking, negating an innate quality, naming, supplication, deserving, arriving, facing, bringing a thing, and differentiating (like this). Examples: *adnaytuhu* (I brought him near), *a'jabani al-makan* (the place pleased me), *aghadda al-ba'ir* (the camel was fattened), *ahlaytu fulanan* (I made so-and-so sweet), *aqbaltu fulanan* (I faced so-and-so), *ashkaytu al-rajul* (I complained about the man), *ahmadtu fulanan* (I praised so-and-so), *a'shartu al-darahim* (I gave a tenth of the dirhams), *asbahna* (we entered the morning), *ashma'a al-qawm* (the people were unlucky), *ahzanahu* in the sense of *hazzanahu* (it saddened him), *arqala* (he hurried), *aqsha'a al-sahab* (the clouds dispersed, the reciprocal of *qasha'a al-rih al-sahab*, the wind scattered the clouds), *aftara* (he broke his fast, reciprocal of *fattartuhu*), *ittala'tu 'alayhim* (I came upon them), *astarih* (I rest), *akhta'tuhu* (I called him mistaken), *asqaytuhu* (I gave him drink), *ahsada al-zar'* (the crop was harvested), *aghfaltuhu* (my heedlessness reached him), *affaftuhu* (I faced him with "uff", in this manner, and similar to this). Some said *af'ala* is *fa'ala*. Also cited as an example of facing is their saying *asqaytuhu*, meaning I faced him with your saying "suqyan laka" (watering to you). *Kaththartu* means I brought the abundant. *Ashraqat al-shams* means it shone, and *shara-qat* means it rose.

The *ta'* attached to *an'amta* is the pronoun of the masculine singular addressee. It is a letter in *anta* (you), and the two pronouns together form a compound.

﴿Upon them﴾: *'ala* is a preposition according to most grammarians, except when it is preceded by *min* (from), or in expressions like *hawwin 'alayka* (take it easy on yourself). Sibawayh's view is that when it governs a noun of place (*ism zarf*), it is not counted among the prepositions. For this reason he did not count it among the prepositions, and a group of our later companions agreed with him. Its meaning is elevation, literally or figuratively. It may have the sense of *'an* (about), *ba'* (with), *fi* (in), accompaniment, causation, *min* (from), and it may be extra. Examples of its extra use: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman: 26]; ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqara: 253]. After *'ala* there is some dispute. ﴿It is incumbent upon me that I should not say﴾ [al-A'raf: 105]. ﴿Over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾. ﴿And gave wealth despite love for it﴾ [al-Baqara: 177]. ﴿That you may glorify Allah for what He has guided you to﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. ﴿Guardians﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5]. ﴿Except upon their spouses﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6].

A line of poetry:
*Allah refused except that the acacia of Malik*
*over all the branches of the thorny trees stands out.*
That is: stands out, all the branches of the thorny trees.

*Hum* is the pronoun of the third-person masculine plural rational. It can occupy the position of nominative, accusative, or genitive. The lexicographers related ten readings of *'alayhim*: a *dammah* on the *ha'* with the *mim* sukun, which is the reading of Hamza. A *kasrah* on the *ha'* with the *mim* sukun, which is the reading of the majority. A *kasrah* on the *ha'* and *mim* with a *ya'* after it, which is the reading of al-Hasan. Ibn Mujahid added that it is also the reading of Umar ibn Fa'id, and similarly without the *ya'*, which is the reading of Amr ibn Fa'id. A *kasrah* on the *ha'*, a *dammah* on the *mim*, and a *waw* after it, which is the reading of Ibn Kathir, and Qalun with a variant from him. A *kasrah* on the *ha'*, a *dammah* on the *mim* without a *waw*, and a *dammah* on the *ha'* and *mim* with a *waw* after it, which is the reading of al-A'raj and al-Khaffaf from Abu Amr. Similarly without a *waw*, with a *dammah* on the *ha'* and a *kasrah* on the *mim* with a *ya'* after it. Similarly without a *ya'*. Both have been recited. (The clarification of these readings in writing and vocalization:) *'alayhim, 'alayhim, 'alayhimu, 'alayhimu, 'alayhimi, 'alayhimi, 'alayhum, 'alayhumi, 'alayhum, 'alayhumu.* Their summary is: a *dammah* on the *ha'* with a sukun on the *mim*, or a *dammah* with full vowel-prolongation, or without it; or a *kasrah* with full vowel-prolongation or without it; a *kasrah* on the *ha'* with a sukun on the *mim*, or with full prolongation, or without it; or a *dammah* with full prolongation or without it. The justification of these readings is mentioned in grammar.

*Ihdina*: its form is the form of the imperative, but its meaning is request and desire. The jurists of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) mentioned fifteen interpretations for this type of form. The original function of this form is to indicate a request, not immediacy, not repetition, and not obligation. Is the meaning of *ihdina*: guide us, make us succeed, put us forward, inspire us, clarify for us, or make us firm? These are opinions, most of them from Ibn Abbas, and the last of them from Ali and Ubayy. Thabit al-Bunani recited *basir-na al-sirat* (show us the path). The meaning of *al-sirat* is the Qur'an, said by Ali and Ibn Abbas. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that it is narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he explained it as the Book of Allah, or faith and its branches, or Islam and its laws, or the moderate way, or the way of the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr and Umar. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah and al-Hasan. Or the way of Hajj, said by Fudayl ibn Iyad. Or the sunnahs, said by Uthman. Or the way to Paradise, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Or the way of the Sunnah and the community, said by al-Qushayri. Or the way of fear and hope, said by al-Tirmidhi. Or the bridge over Hell, said by Amr ibn Ubayd.

Opinions have been related from the Sufis concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. Among them is the saying of some of them: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ with absorption in the path, so that one is not tied to the path. The saying of al-Junayd is that asking for guidance at the time of bewilderment is a manifestation of the eternal attributes, so they asked for guidance to the attributes of servanthood, so that they would not become absorbed in the eternal attributes. These statements are repugnant to the wording, but they have a taste and perception regarding what they mention that we have not yet reached. The exegeses have been filled with their statements, and we touch upon some of them so that it is not thought that we left mention of them because we were not aware of them. Al-Fakhr al-Razi refuted those who said that the straight path is the Qur'an or Islam and its laws. He said: Because what is intended by ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ is from among the earlier people, and for them there was no Qur'an nor Islam. By Islam he means this Islamic religion specific to obligations that had not preceded it. This refutation can only work if it is established that those upon whom Allah bestowed favor are earlier people. The statements concerning the interpretation of ﴿those upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾ will come. The connection of *na* with *ihdi* is appropriate for *na'budu* and *nasta'in* (we worship and we seek help), because when the speaker reported that he and those with him worship Allah and seek His help, he asked for guidance for himself and for them to the clear path, because by being guided to it their worship becomes valid. Do you not see that one who is not guided to the way that leads to his goal cannot reach his goal? Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak recited: *sirat-an mustaqim-an* without definiteness. Ja'far al-Sadiq recited: *sirat mustaqim* with the *idafa* (construct), meaning the straight religion. According to the reading of al-Hasan and al-Dahhak, *sirat alladhina* is an apposition of indefinite to definite (*badal ma'rifa min nakira*), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], ﴿the path of Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 53]. According to the reading of al-Sadiq and the readings of the majority, it is an apposition of definite to definite (*badal ma'rifa min ma'rifa*): *sirat alladhina* is *badal shay' min shay'* (an apposition of one thing from another). Both refer to one and the same thing. It was brought for clarification, because when it was mentioned before ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ there was some vagueness in it, so He specified it with His saying ﴿the path of those﴾, so that the one whose guidance is sought would have been mentioned twice.
