By this the apposition becomes an attribution to a path of those upon whom Allah bestowed favor, which makes it firmer and more emphatic. This is the purpose of this type of apposition. And because it repeats the governing verb, it becomes in estimation two sentences, and the emphasis of two sentences is not hidden. It is as if they repeated the request for guidance.

[p. 28] Among the strange opinions is that the second path is not the first but something other than it, as though a conjunction (ḥarf al-ʿaṭf) had been read there. There is disagreement about what this is. It was said: it is knowledge of God and understanding from Him, as stated by Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad. It was said: it is adherence to the obligations and following the sunnah (the prophetic practice). It was said: it is the agreement of the inner state with the outer in the abundance of blessing. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And He has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward﴾ [Luqman: 20]. And Ibn Masʿud, ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read: "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" (ṣirāṭa man anʿamta ʿalayhim).

The ones upon whom favour is bestowed here are the prophets, or the angels, or the community of Moses and Jesus who did not change [their religion], or the Prophet (ﷺ), or the prophets, the truthful (ṣiddīqūn), the martyrs and the righteous, or the believers, as stated by Ibn ʿAbbas. Or the prophets and the believers, or the Muslims, as stated by Wakiʿ. These are opinions, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributed many of them to their sayers. He said: Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority said: He intended the path of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, deriving this from the verse of al-Nisāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: they are the believers. al-Ḥasan said: they are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). A group said: they are the believers among the Children of Israel. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the companions of Moses before they changed [their religion]. Qatada said: the prophets specifically. Abu al-ʿĀliya said: Muhammad (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and ʿUmar. The end of the summary.

He did not restrict the favour, so that it would include all favours; I mean the generality of the substitution. It was said: He bestowed favour upon them by creating them for happiness. It was said: by saving them from ruin. It was said: by guidance and following the Messenger. Many restrictions other than these have been transmitted from the Sufis, but there is nothing in the wording that indicates the specification of any particular restriction.

It has been disputed whether God has a favour upon the disbeliever. The Muʿtazila affirmed it, and others denied it.

The position of ʿalayhim is in the accusative (naṣb) grammatically, and so is every prepositional phrase (ḥarf jarr) that is attached to a verb, or what functions like one, when the verb is not in the passive. The form anʿamta in the active voice is an appeal for kindness (istiʿṭāf), for the acceptance of the request made in supplication for guidance and its attainment. That is, we ask You for guidance, since Your favour has preceded; so from Your favour is the answering of our request and our desire. This is like asking a person for the fulfilment of a need while reminding him that it is his habit to be benevolent by fulfilling needs; this makes the request more binding and more likely to be granted. The inversion of the subject with the pronoun is the most common usage, and it is permissible to keep it with the pronoun in another dialect. The content of this sentence is a request for the continuation of guidance on the path of those upon whom God has bestowed favour, because whoever has come forth [in this way] praises God and informs that he worships Him and seeks His help; guidance has already been attained for him, but he asks for its continuance and persistence.

﴿Ghayr﴾ is always singular and masculine; when it is intended for the feminine, it is permissible to make the verb masculine by agreement with the wording, or feminine by agreement with the meaning. Its meaning is difference in some respect. Its original function is as a qualifier (waṣf); it is used for exception (istithnāʾ), and it necessarily requires an annexation (iḍāfa), verbal or semantic. Prefixing al- to it is an error, and it does not become definite even when annexed to a definite noun. The view of Ibn al-Sarrāj is that when the thing differing is one, it becomes definite by its annexation to it. It has been transmitted from Sibawayh that every annexation that is not pure (ghayr maḥḍa) may be intended to give definiteness, and then it becomes pure, and so ghayr becomes definite at that point with what it is annexed to, if that is definite. The detailed working out of all this is in the books of grammar.

The rhetoricians (al-bayāniyyūn) claim that ghayr or mithl, when they are the subject of a predication, are almost obligatorily placed first. They say, for example, "Your other (ghayruka) is feared for his injustice" and "Your like (mithluka) will be for noble deeds," and similar expressions in which mithl is not intended to refer to a person other than the one it is annexed to. Rather, they mean that everyone who is like him in the quality is by logical necessity and the requirement of custom expected to do what is mentioned. The poet's line:

"Other than me, most people are deceived."

His purpose is that he is not one of those who are deceived and deluded. This meaning does not hold in these two cases if they are not placed first, as in: "Your like will be for noble deeds," and "Most people are deceived other than me." You see the sentence then reversed from its proper order.

﴿Those upon whom is wrath﴾: anger (ghaḍab) is a change of disposition due to something disliked, and it may be applied to aversion (iʿrāḍ), because aversion is one of its fruits.

﴿Lā﴾ is a particle that is used for negation, for prohibition, and as a supplementary (zāʾida) particle; it is not a noun, contrary to the view of the Kufans.

﴿Nor of those who go astray﴾: al-ḍalāl means ruin and concealment: "the milk went astray in the water." It was said: its root meaning is disappearance. ﴿In a Book, my Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52]. "I lost (ḍalaltu) the thing" means I did not know the place where I had put it. "I caused the thing to go astray" (aḍlaltu al-shayʾ) means I lost it. ﴿And He causes their deeds to go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1]. "He went astray" (ḍalla) means he forgot and neglected; ﴿and I am among those who go astray﴾ [Yusuf: 20]; ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [al-Baqara: 282]. Going astray is following a course other than the intended one: "he strayed from the road" means he took a route other than its main track. Going astray is also bewilderment and hesitation, and from this is said of a smooth stone that the water moves back and forth in the valley: ḍalḍalahu. The meaning of going astray in the Qur'an has been explained as lack of knowledge of the details of matters, and as love; this will come in its places.

The genitive (jarr) in ghayr is the reading of the majority. Al-Khalil transmitted from Ibn Kathir the accusative (naṣb), and it is the reading of ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAlī and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. The genitive is then either a substitution (badal) from alladhīna, according to Abu ʿAlī, or from the pronoun in ʿalayhim; both are weak, because ghayr originally functions as a qualifier, and substitution with a qualifier is weak. Or it is a qualifier (naʿt) according to Sibawayh; in that case ghayr becomes definite by what it is annexed to, since it is definite according to what Sibawayh transmitted, in that every annexation that is not pure may become pure and so become definite, except in the attributive adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha). Or it is according to what Ibn al-Sarrāj held, since ghayr has been used for something specific, not general. Or because alladhīna is intended as a class, not particular people. They said: just as they describe the definite with the generic alif-lam by a clause. This demolishes what they had resolved upon, namely that the definite may only be qualified by the definite. I do not choose this view, and the refutation of its unsoundness is in grammar. The accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ʿalayhim, which is the preferred view, or from alladhīna, as al-Mahdawi and others said, is an error, because a circumstantial from the genitive-annexed noun whose place has no grammatical position is not permitted. Or it is an exception (istithnāʾ), as said by al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and others; it is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), since the preceding wording does not include it. al-Farrāʾ prohibited it because of the lā in ﴿nor of those who go astray﴾, and he allowed in the accusative only the circumstantial. He said: because lā is not added except when negation precedes it, as in the poet's line:

"The Messenger of God would not approve their deed, nor would the two good ones, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar."

Whoever holds the exception makes lā a connective particle (ṣila), that is, a supplementary particle like it in the words of the Exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12], and the line of the rajaz poet:

"So I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking."

And the line of al-Aḥwaṣ:

"And they blame me in play that I do not love it, while play has a persistent, unheedless caller."

al-Ṭabari said: i.e., that you mock, and that I love it. Others said: its meaning is the intention that I do not love it, so lā is in it a fixed negation, not supplementary. They also argued for its supplementary use with a verse recited by the commentators:

"His generosity refused, not avarice, and it hastened him, yes, from a youth who does not prevent generosity from killing him."

They claimed that lā is supplementary and al-bukhl is the object of abā, i.e., his generosity refused avarice. There is no proof in this; rather the more evident view is that lā is the object of abā, and that the word lā is not connected to it, and it becomes a verbal predication (isnād lafẓī). That is why he said: "it hastened him, yes," making yes the subject of "hastened," which is a verbal predication, and al-bukhl is either a substitution for lā or an object of purpose. It was said: ghayr is in the accusative by an implied verb "I mean" (aʿnī), which he attributed to al-Khalil; this is an easy estimation. ʿAlayhim is in the place of the nominative by al-maghḍūb, which is the grammatical subject of a passive verb whose agent is unspecified. Concerning the placement of the prepositional phrase in the position of the agent when it is omitted, there is disagreement mentioned in grammar. Among the subtleties of its issues is a question in which one dispenses with the predicate of the subject, mentioned in grammar.

The lā in ﴿nor of those who go astray﴾ is for emphasizing the meaning of negation, because ghayr contains negation; it is as if it were said: "Not those upon whom is wrath, nor those who go astray." It specifies its entry through the conjunction upon ﴿those upon whom is wrath﴾, because of the affinity with ghayr, and so that by omitting it one would not suppose that ﴿those who go astray﴾ is conjoined to alladhīna. ʿUmar and Ubayy read: "wa-ghayri al-ḍāllīn" (with the genitive), and it is transmitted from them that in both places the raʾ may be read in the accusative or the genitive. It indicates that those upon whom is wrath are other than those who go astray, and emphasis in it is further away, while emphasis in lā is closer. Because the meaning of ghayr is close to the meaning of lā, al-Zamakhshari brought a question to demonstrate their closeness. He said: "You say: 'I, Zayd, am other than one who strikes,' although 'I, Zayd, am like one who strikes' is impermissible, because it is equivalent to your saying 'I, Zayd, am not one who strikes.'" He means that when the governing word is genitive by annexation, its complement may not precede it or the annexed noun. But they were lenient with the governing word annexed to ghayr, so they permitted placing its complement before ghayr, treating ghayr as not being like lā. So just as the complement of what follows lā may not precede it, similarly with ghayr. Al-Zamakhshari presented it as a settled question, one finished with, in order to strengthen the correspondence between ghayr and lā, since he mentioned no disagreement in it. This view to which al-Zamakhshari went is very weak; he built it upon the permissibility of "I, Zayd, am not striking," and on the preposing of the complement of what follows lā over it there are three positions mentioned in grammar. That a word is close in meaning to another does not justify applying its rules to it, and a construction is not established except by hearing from the Arabs, and "I, Zayd, am other than striking" has not been heard. Our companions (the grammarians of our school) have mentioned the view of those who permitted this and refuted it. Some of them estimated for ﴿ghayr al-maghḍūb﴾ an implied noun, saying: the estimate is "other than the path of those upon whom is wrath," and they stated this estimate without restricting it to the genitive or accusative of ghayr. This is only possible with the accusative of ghayr, so that it would be a qualifier of "the path" (al-ṣirāṭ), and this is weak because the substitution precedes the qualifier, whereas the norm is the reverse. Or it is a qualifier of the substitution, which is ﴿the path of those﴾; or a substitution of al-ṣirāṭ, or of ﴿the path of those﴾, and this involves repeated substitution. This is an issue on which I have not found the words of anyone, except that they mentioned this in the substitution of the vocative. Or it is a circumstantial of the first or second path.

Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read: "wa-lā al-ḍaʾlīn" (with a hamza), replacing the alif with a hamza to avoid the meeting of two quiescent letters. Abu Zayd transmitted "daʾba" and "shaʾba" in the Book of Hamz, and from it came some words of this kind. Nevertheless, this substitution is not a general rule, because it did not occur frequently enough to require analogy; the grammarians stated explicitly that it is not analogical. Abu Zayd said: I heard ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recite ﴿On that day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ [al-Rahman: 39], and I thought he had made a grammatical error, until I heard from the Arabs "daʾba" and "shaʾba." Abu al-Fath said: upon this dialect is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"When the spears are reddened with fresh blood."

And the verse of another:

"As for the earth, if its blackness has become clear, and if its whiteness has become dark."

**Part 3 of 3**

In line with what Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said, that it is a dialect in which this is applicable, the bestowal of blessing is placed in the relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and the anger in the relative clause of *al* (the definite article). This is because the relative clause of *alladhina* is a verb, so its time is specific, whereas the relative clause of *al* is a noun, so its time is indefinite. The intended meaning is the request for guidance to the path of those upon whom God's blessing has been established and confirmed. For the same reason, He used the verb in the past tense and the noun in the relative clause of *anna*, so that it would encompass all times. He also used the passive form, because the one from whom guidance is requested, and to whom blessing is attributed, is not a fitting object for the attribution of anger. This is a context of gentleness, kindness and humility in seeking benevolence, so it is not appropriate to confront him with the description of retribution. Also, so that "those who have incurred anger" would serve as a preparation for ending the surah with "those who have gone astray," by conjoining one relative pronoun to another of the same kind, in agreement with the final rhymes of the verses. By "blessing" is meant religious blessing. "Those who have incurred anger" and "those who have gone astray" are general terms applying to everyone who has incurred anger and gone astray.

It has been said: "Those who have incurred anger" are the Jews, and "those who have gone astray" are the Christians. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. This was also reported from Adi ibn Hatim, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). If this is authentic, it is obligatory to adopt it. It has also been said that they are the Jews and the polytheists, and it has been said otherwise.

Some restrictions have been reported in the books of tafsir concerning anger and going astray, from the Sufis, which the wording does not indicate. Such as the saying of some of them: "﴿other than those who have incurred anger﴾" refers to neglecting good manners during the performance of service to Him, and "﴿nor of those who have gone astray﴾" refers to regarding that (service) as one's own achievement. And other things have been said besides this.

Anger from God, exalted is He, means the will to exact retribution from the disobedient, because He knows the servant before his creation and before the disobedience proceeds from him. Thus it is one of the attributes of the essence (*sifat al-dhat*, attributes belonging to the divine essence itself). Or it means the infliction of punishment upon him, and thus it is one of the attributes of action (*sifat al-af'al*, attributes pertaining to divine acts). Anger was placed before going astray, although anger is a consequence of going astray: one who strays from the truth is angered at him, and it is placed next to the blessing. The relevance of mentioning it is a correspondence, because blessing is opposed by retribution, whereas going astray is not opposed to blessing. Blessing is the conveyance of good to the one blessed, and retribution is the conveyance of harm to the one against whom anger is directed. Between them there is a semantic antithesis. There is also in it a harmony of rhyme, because His saying "﴿nor of those who have gone astray﴾" is the end of the surah, so it harmonizes with the final verses. Had anger and its object been placed later, it would not have harmonized with the final verses.

The conjunction used was the all-inclusive *wa* (and), which does not indicate precedence or subsequence, because this meaning is achieved through the difference between the two descriptions being combined: the anger directed at him and the going astray, for the one upon whom God has bestowed blessing. Even if the words are interpreted as referring to the Jews and the Christians, the precedence is either for chronological reasons or for the intensity of enmity, because the Jews are older and more intensely hostile than the Christians.

In the course of the tafsir of this noble surah, many benefits from the science of eloquence (*'ilm al-bayan*) have emerged, which can only be extracted by one who has delved deeply into the understanding of the Arabic language, has been granted a generous share of the science of literature, and is knowledgeable in the elegance of speech, capable of composing graceful prose and verse. As for one who has no acquaintance with the speech of the Arabs, whose nature has become dull even to a single passage of literature, his hearing is closed to this discipline and his mind is far from this purpose.

They have said: In this noble surah there are several kinds of eloquence and rhetoric:

(The first kind): the excellence of the opening and the brilliance of the beginning. If its first verse is "﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾" according to the view of one who counts it as part of the surah, then that alone is enough excellence, since its beginning opens with the name of God. If its first verse is "﴿Praise be to God﴾," then praise of God and commendation of Him by what is worthy of Him, and describing Him with His exalted attributes, is the finest way to begin speech, and it is placed before prose and verse. The opening with praise recurs in many surahs. Openings are divided into good and bad, and the good into apparent and hidden, as has been classified in the science of rhetorical embellishment (*'ilm al-badi'*).

(The second kind): exaggeration in praise, and this is due to the generality of the definite article *al* in "praise" according to the interpretation already mentioned.

(The third kind): the shifting of discourse (*talwin al-khitab*), according to the saying of some of them. For he mentioned that "Praise be to God" has the form of a declarative statement but its meaning is a command, like His saying "﴿there is no doubt in it﴾," whose meaning is a prohibition.

(The fourth kind): specification by the *lam* in "for God" (*lillah*), since it indicates that all praises are specifically His, because He alone deserves them. And by the genitive construction in "Master of the Day of Judgment," because on that day dominion and kingdoms cease for anyone other than Him, and He alone holds sovereignty and possession. He, exalted is He, said: "﴿To whom belongs the dominion this Day?﴾" And because on that Day no one other than Him recompenses deeds.

(The fifth kind): ellipsis (*al-hadhf*). On the reading of one who puts "praise" in the accusative, it is apparent, and it has already been discussed whether it is to be supplied from the word "praise" or from something other than its wording. Some of them have said: Among it is the deletion of the governing element, which in reality is a predicate of "praise," and which is supplied as "existing" or "established." He said: Among it is the deletion of "path" in His saying "﴿other than those who have incurred anger﴾," the implied meaning being "other than the path of those who have incurred anger, and other than the path of those who have gone astray." Among it is also the deletion of "chapter" if we supply the governing element of "praise," when we put it in the accusative, as "remember" or "recite," so the implied meaning is "recite the chapter of praise." As for one who restricts "the Most Merciful," "the Most Compassionate," "we worship," "we seek help," "You have blessed," "those who have incurred anger," and "those who have gone astray," he will find many elisions in this surah.

(The sixth kind): anteriority and posteriority (*al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir*). This occurs in His saying "we worship," "we seek help," "those who have incurred anger," and "those who have gone astray." The discussion of this has already preceded.

(The seventh kind): explanation (*al-tafsir*), also called clarification after ambiguity. This occurs in the apposition of "﴿the path of those﴾" to "﴿the straight path﴾."

(The eighth kind): the shift of grammatical person (*al-iltifat*). This occurs in "﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾" and "﴿guide us﴾."

(The ninth kind): the request for something, where the intended meaning is not its attainment but its continuation. This occurs in "﴿guide us﴾."

(The tenth kind): the enumeration of attributes, to explain a particularity in the one described, or for praise or blame.

(The eleventh kind): rhymed prose (*al-taj'i*). In this surah there is parallel rhymed prose (*al-taj'i al-mutawazi*), which is the agreement of the last two words in measure and final rhyme. Examples are His saying "﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾," "﴿guide us to the straight path﴾," and His saying "﴿we seek help﴾" with "﴿nor of those who have gone astray﴾."

Our discussion of the tafsir of al-Fatiha has ended.

Al-Hasan disliked calling it "Umm al-Kitab" (the Mother of the Book), and Ibn Sirin disliked calling it "Umm al-Qur'an" (the Mother of the Qur'an), but the majority permitted it. There is consensus that it consists of seven verses, except for an anomalous view from one whose dissent is not taken into account. The Meccan and Kufan scholars of counting, the majority, counted "﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾" as a verse, but did not count "﴿those upon whom You have bestowed blessing﴾." Other counters, including Ibn Kathir among the reciters of Mecca and Kufa, did not count it as a verse, but counted "﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed blessing﴾" as a verse. Amr ibn Ubayd was anomalous in making "﴿You alone we worship﴾" a verse, so on his count it has eight verses. Husayn al-Ju'fi was anomalous in claiming it has six verses. Ibn Atiyya said: God's saying, exalted is He, "﴿We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾" is the decisive proof in this matter. They did not differ that the basmala at the beginning of every surah is not a verse, except that Ibn al-Mubarak was anomalous and said that it is a verse in every surah. I do not know what criterion is considered in the length of a verse, by which we would distinguish a verse from non-verse.

The exegetes mentioned the number of letters of al-Fatiha and mentioned a cause of its revelation that does not count as a cause of revelation. They mentioned hadiths about the virtues of "﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾," God knows best about them. They also mentioned things about the basmala that do not count as causes. They mentioned that al-Fatiha is called "al-Hamd" (the Praise), "Fatihat al-Kitab" (the Opening of the Book), "Umm al-Kitab" (the Mother of the Book), "al-Sab' al-Mathani" (the Seven Oft-Repeated), "al-Waqiya" (the Protector), "al-Kafiya" (the Sufficient), "al-Shifa" (the Cure), "al-Shafiya" (the Healing), "al-Ruqya" (the Incantation), "al-Kanz" (the Treasure), "al-Asas" (the Foundation), "al-Nur" (the Light), "Surat al-Salat" (the Surah of Prayer), "Surat Ta'lim al-Mas'ala" (the Surah Teaching the Request), "Surat al-Munaja" (the Surah of Intimate Supplication), and "Surat al-Tafwid" (the Surah of Surrender). They mentioned that the hadiths about the virtues of al-Fatiha, and all discussion of this, belong to the category of supplementary remarks (*al-tadhyilat*), and are not part of the science of tafsir, except what concerns the specification of something ambiguous, or the cause of revelation, or abrogation, by what is authentically reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Such matters are necessary for the science of tafsir. Likewise they discussed "Amin," its dialects, the disagreement over its meaning and its ruling in prayer, though it is not part of the Qur'an. Therefore we have passed over discussion of it entirely, just as we left aside discussion of the seeking of refuge (*al-isti'adha*) at the beginning of the book. Exegetes have lengthened their books with matters outside the science of tafsir, which we have omitted from this book of ours, since our aim is what we indicated in the introduction. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 1, verses 6–7 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿Guide us﴾. *Al-hidaya* (guidance) means direction, indication, and going ahead. From it comes *al-hawadi* (the leading animals of a caravan). It also means clarification, as in ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. It may also mean inspiration, as in ﴿He gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50]. The exegetes said its meaning is that He inspired all animals toward their benefits. It may also mean calling, as in ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], meaning a caller. The basic form of *hada* is that it reaches its second object with *li* (to), as in ﴿He guides to what is most upright﴾ [al-Isra: 9], or with *ila* (to), as in ﴿You guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Then its usage widens so that it takes the object directly, as in ﴿Guide us to the path﴾. *Na* is the pronoun of the speaker when accompanied by others, or of the speaker's own self in the majestic sense. It can occupy the position of nominative, accusative, or genitive.

﴿The path﴾: *al-tariq* (the road). Its original form is with *sin*, from *al-sarth*, which means swallowing. From this the road was called *laqm* (a swallowing). Qunbul and Ruways recited it with *sin*, in accordance with the original form. Replacing its *sin* with *sad* is the most eloquent form, the dialect of Quraysh, and the majority recited it this way. It is also how it was written in the *Imam* (the standard codex). Pronouncing it as *zay* is a dialect transmitted by al-Asma'i from Abu Amr. Pronouncing it with *ishmam* (a slight hint of *zay*) is the dialect of Qays, and Hamza recited it this way with variations and detailed differences among his transmitters. Abu Ya'la said: It is transmitted from Abu Amr also: *sin*, *sad*, and *al-mudari'a* (a blend) between *zay* and *sad*. It was transmitted from him by al-Uryan from Abu Sufyan. Al-Asma'i transmitted from Abu Amr that he recited it with a pure *zay*. Some linguists said: What al-Asma'i reported in this recitation is an error on his part. He only heard Abu Amr recite it with *al-mudari'a* and mistook it for *zay*. Al-Asma'i was not a grammarian, so he cannot be trusted in this. Abu Ali related this statement from Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid. Abu Ja'far al-Tusi said in his exegesis, and he is one of the imams of the Imamiyya: *Al-sirat* with *sad* is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is the good dialect. Most Arabs make it *sin*. *Zay* is the dialect of Udhra, Ka'b, and Bani al-Qayn. Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid said: This recitation indicates that the recitation of one who recites between *zay* and *sad* is an effort to produce a letter between two letters, which is difficult on the tongue, and it is not a letter upon which speech is built, nor is it one of the letters of the alphabet. I do not deny that it is from the speech of eloquent Arabs, but *sad* is more eloquent and more widespread. It is used as both masculine and feminine, and its masculine use is more common. Abu Ja'far al-Tusi said: The people of the Hijaz use *al-sirat* as feminine, like *al-tariq*, *al-sabil*, *al-zuqaq*, and *al-suq*. The Banu Tamim use all of these as masculine. In the plural of abundance it is *surut*, like *kitab* and *kutub*. In the plural of paucity its analogical form is *asrita*, like *himar* and *ahmira*. This is when *al-sirat* is masculine. When it is feminine, its analogical form is *af'ul*, like *dhira'* and *adhru'*, and *shimal* and *ashmul*. Zayd ibn Ali, al-Dahhak, and Nasr ibn Ali, from al-Hasan, recited: *Ihdina sirat-an mustaqim-an* (Guide us to a straight path), with tanwin (nunation) and without the definite article, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], ﴿the path of Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 53].

﴿Straight﴾: *istaqama* is *istaf'ala* in the sense of the bare verb without augmentation. This is one of the meanings of *istaf'ala*: that it has the sense of the bare verb, which is *qama*. *Al-qiyam* is standing upright and being level, without crookedness.

* *

﴿The path of those﴾: *alladhina* is a relative pronoun. The more eloquent form is with *ya* in all its three cases. Some Arabs make it with *waw* in the nominative case. Using it with the *nun* dropped is permissible. Some restricted this to poetic necessity, but if it is not for restriction, it is permissible in other cases. The dropping of the *alif-lam* from it has been heard, and they say *alladhina*. The matter of how it is defined is a disputed point discussed in grammar. *Alladhina* is specific to rational beings, unlike *alladhi*, which applies to one who has knowledge and to other things.

﴿You have blessed﴾: *al-ni'ma* is ease and softness of life. For this reason the south wind is called *al-nu'ma* because of the softness of its blowing, and the ostrich is called *al-na'ama* because of the softness of its arrow. *Ni'ma* means one who is in blessing. *An'amtu 'aynahu* means I gladdened his eye. *An'ama 'alayhi* means he exceeded in favoring him. The *hamza* in *an'ama* is for making the thing possessor of what is derived from it, but it has been given the meaning of bestowing favor, so it takes *'ala* (upon). Its original usage is transitive without a preposition: *an'amtuhu*, meaning I made him a possessor of blessing. This is one of the meanings of *af'ala*, which has twenty-four meanings. This is one of them. The others are: transitivity, multiplicity, becoming, assistance, exposure, negation, attaining the thing in the sense of what is derived from it, reaching a number, time, or place, agreeing with the triliteral form, sufficiency from it, reciprocity of one verb with another, attacking, negating an innate quality, naming, supplication, deserving, arriving, facing, bringing a thing, and differentiating (like this). Examples: *adnaytuhu* (I brought him near), *a'jabani al-makan* (the place pleased me), *aghadda al-ba'ir* (the camel was fattened), *ahlaytu fulanan* (I made so-and-so sweet), *aqbaltu fulanan* (I faced so-and-so), *ashkaytu al-rajul* (I complained about the man), *ahmadtu fulanan* (I praised so-and-so), *a'shartu al-darahim* (I gave a tenth of the dirhams), *asbahna* (we entered the morning), *ashma'a al-qawm* (the people were unlucky), *ahzanahu* in the sense of *hazzanahu* (it saddened him), *arqala* (he hurried), *aqsha'a al-sahab* (the clouds dispersed, the reciprocal of *qasha'a al-rih al-sahab*, the wind scattered the clouds), *aftara* (he broke his fast, reciprocal of *fattartuhu*), *ittala'tu 'alayhim* (I came upon them), *astarih* (I rest), *akhta'tuhu* (I called him mistaken), *asqaytuhu* (I gave him drink), *ahsada al-zar'* (the crop was harvested), *aghfaltuhu* (my heedlessness reached him), *affaftuhu* (I faced him with "uff", in this manner, and similar to this). Some said *af'ala* is *fa'ala*. Also cited as an example of facing is their saying *asqaytuhu*, meaning I faced him with your saying "suqyan laka" (watering to you). *Kaththartu* means I brought the abundant. *Ashraqat al-shams* means it shone, and *shara-qat* means it rose.

The *ta'* attached to *an'amta* is the pronoun of the masculine singular addressee. It is a letter in *anta* (you), and the two pronouns together form a compound.

﴿Upon them﴾: *'ala* is a preposition according to most grammarians, except when it is preceded by *min* (from), or in expressions like *hawwin 'alayka* (take it easy on yourself). Sibawayh's view is that when it governs a noun of place (*ism zarf*), it is not counted among the prepositions. For this reason he did not count it among the prepositions, and a group of our later companions agreed with him. Its meaning is elevation, literally or figuratively. It may have the sense of *'an* (about), *ba'* (with), *fi* (in), accompaniment, causation, *min* (from), and it may be extra. Examples of its extra use: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman: 26]; ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqara: 253]. After *'ala* there is some dispute. ﴿It is incumbent upon me that I should not say﴾ [al-A'raf: 105]. ﴿Over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾. ﴿And gave wealth despite love for it﴾ [al-Baqara: 177]. ﴿That you may glorify Allah for what He has guided you to﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. ﴿Guardians﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5]. ﴿Except upon their spouses﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6].

A line of poetry:
*Allah refused except that the acacia of Malik*
*over all the branches of the thorny trees stands out.*
That is: stands out, all the branches of the thorny trees.

*Hum* is the pronoun of the third-person masculine plural rational. It can occupy the position of nominative, accusative, or genitive. The lexicographers related ten readings of *'alayhim*: a *dammah* on the *ha'* with the *mim* sukun, which is the reading of Hamza. A *kasrah* on the *ha'* with the *mim* sukun, which is the reading of the majority. A *kasrah* on the *ha'* and *mim* with a *ya'* after it, which is the reading of al-Hasan. Ibn Mujahid added that it is also the reading of Umar ibn Fa'id, and similarly without the *ya'*, which is the reading of Amr ibn Fa'id. A *kasrah* on the *ha'*, a *dammah* on the *mim*, and a *waw* after it, which is the reading of Ibn Kathir, and Qalun with a variant from him. A *kasrah* on the *ha'*, a *dammah* on the *mim* without a *waw*, and a *dammah* on the *ha'* and *mim* with a *waw* after it, which is the reading of al-A'raj and al-Khaffaf from Abu Amr. Similarly without a *waw*, with a *dammah* on the *ha'* and a *kasrah* on the *mim* with a *ya'* after it. Similarly without a *ya'*. Both have been recited. (The clarification of these readings in writing and vocalization:) *'alayhim, 'alayhim, 'alayhimu, 'alayhimu, 'alayhimi, 'alayhimi, 'alayhum, 'alayhumi, 'alayhum, 'alayhumu.* Their summary is: a *dammah* on the *ha'* with a sukun on the *mim*, or a *dammah* with full vowel-prolongation, or without it; or a *kasrah* with full vowel-prolongation or without it; a *kasrah* on the *ha'* with a sukun on the *mim*, or with full prolongation, or without it; or a *dammah* with full prolongation or without it. The justification of these readings is mentioned in grammar.

*Ihdina*: its form is the form of the imperative, but its meaning is request and desire. The jurists of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) mentioned fifteen interpretations for this type of form. The original function of this form is to indicate a request, not immediacy, not repetition, and not obligation. Is the meaning of *ihdina*: guide us, make us succeed, put us forward, inspire us, clarify for us, or make us firm? These are opinions, most of them from Ibn Abbas, and the last of them from Ali and Ubayy. Thabit al-Bunani recited *basir-na al-sirat* (show us the path). The meaning of *al-sirat* is the Qur'an, said by Ali and Ibn Abbas. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that it is narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he explained it as the Book of Allah, or faith and its branches, or Islam and its laws, or the moderate way, or the way of the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr and Umar. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah and al-Hasan. Or the way of Hajj, said by Fudayl ibn Iyad. Or the sunnahs, said by Uthman. Or the way to Paradise, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Or the way of the Sunnah and the community, said by al-Qushayri. Or the way of fear and hope, said by al-Tirmidhi. Or the bridge over Hell, said by Amr ibn Ubayd.

Opinions have been related from the Sufis concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. Among them is the saying of some of them: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ with absorption in the path, so that one is not tied to the path. The saying of al-Junayd is that asking for guidance at the time of bewilderment is a manifestation of the eternal attributes, so they asked for guidance to the attributes of servanthood, so that they would not become absorbed in the eternal attributes. These statements are repugnant to the wording, but they have a taste and perception regarding what they mention that we have not yet reached. The exegeses have been filled with their statements, and we touch upon some of them so that it is not thought that we left mention of them because we were not aware of them. Al-Fakhr al-Razi refuted those who said that the straight path is the Qur'an or Islam and its laws. He said: Because what is intended by ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ is from among the earlier people, and for them there was no Qur'an nor Islam. By Islam he means this Islamic religion specific to obligations that had not preceded it. This refutation can only work if it is established that those upon whom Allah bestowed favor are earlier people. The statements concerning the interpretation of ﴿those upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾ will come. The connection of *na* with *ihdi* is appropriate for *na'budu* and *nasta'in* (we worship and we seek help), because when the speaker reported that he and those with him worship Allah and seek His help, he asked for guidance for himself and for them to the clear path, because by being guided to it their worship becomes valid. Do you not see that one who is not guided to the way that leads to his goal cannot reach his goal? Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak recited: *sirat-an mustaqim-an* without definiteness. Ja'far al-Sadiq recited: *sirat mustaqim* with the *idafa* (construct), meaning the straight religion. According to the reading of al-Hasan and al-Dahhak, *sirat alladhina* is an apposition of indefinite to definite (*badal ma'rifa min nakira*), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], ﴿the path of Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 53]. According to the reading of al-Sadiq and the readings of the majority, it is an apposition of definite to definite (*badal ma'rifa min ma'rifa*): *sirat alladhina* is *badal shay' min shay'* (an apposition of one thing from another). Both refer to one and the same thing. It was brought for clarification, because when it was mentioned before ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ there was some vagueness in it, so He specified it with His saying ﴿the path of those﴾, so that the one whose guidance is sought would have been mentioned twice. By this the apposition becomes an attribution to a path of those upon whom Allah bestowed favor, which makes it firmer and more emphatic. This is the purpose of this type of apposition. And because it repeats the governing verb, it becomes in estimation two sentences, and the emphasis of two sentences is not hidden. It is as if they repeated the request for guidance.

[p. 28] Among the strange opinions is that the second path is not the first but something other than it, as though a conjunction (ḥarf al-ʿaṭf) had been read there. There is disagreement about what this is. It was said: it is knowledge of God and understanding from Him, as stated by Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad. It was said: it is adherence to the obligations and following the sunnah (the prophetic practice). It was said: it is the agreement of the inner state with the outer in the abundance of blessing. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And He has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward﴾ [Luqman: 20]. And Ibn Masʿud, ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read: "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" (ṣirāṭa man anʿamta ʿalayhim).

The ones upon whom favour is bestowed here are the prophets, or the angels, or the community of Moses and Jesus who did not change [their religion], or the Prophet (ﷺ), or the prophets, the truthful (ṣiddīqūn), the martyrs and the righteous, or the believers, as stated by Ibn ʿAbbas. Or the prophets and the believers, or the Muslims, as stated by Wakiʿ. These are opinions, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributed many of them to their sayers. He said: Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority said: He intended the path of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, deriving this from the verse of al-Nisāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: they are the believers. al-Ḥasan said: they are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). A group said: they are the believers among the Children of Israel. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the companions of Moses before they changed [their religion]. Qatada said: the prophets specifically. Abu al-ʿĀliya said: Muhammad (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and ʿUmar. The end of the summary.

He did not restrict the favour, so that it would include all favours; I mean the generality of the substitution. It was said: He bestowed favour upon them by creating them for happiness. It was said: by saving them from ruin. It was said: by guidance and following the Messenger. Many restrictions other than these have been transmitted from the Sufis, but there is nothing in the wording that indicates the specification of any particular restriction.

It has been disputed whether God has a favour upon the disbeliever. The Muʿtazila affirmed it, and others denied it.

The position of ʿalayhim is in the accusative (naṣb) grammatically, and so is every prepositional phrase (ḥarf jarr) that is attached to a verb, or what functions like one, when the verb is not in the passive. The form anʿamta in the active voice is an appeal for kindness (istiʿṭāf), for the acceptance of the request made in supplication for guidance and its attainment. That is, we ask You for guidance, since Your favour has preceded; so from Your favour is the answering of our request and our desire. This is like asking a person for the fulfilment of a need while reminding him that it is his habit to be benevolent by fulfilling needs; this makes the request more binding and more likely to be granted. The inversion of the subject with the pronoun is the most common usage, and it is permissible to keep it with the pronoun in another dialect. The content of this sentence is a request for the continuation of guidance on the path of those upon whom God has bestowed favour, because whoever has come forth [in this way] praises God and informs that he worships Him and seeks His help; guidance has already been attained for him, but he asks for its continuance and persistence.

﴿Ghayr﴾ is always singular and masculine; when it is intended for the feminine, it is permissible to make the verb masculine by agreement with the wording, or feminine by agreement with the meaning. Its meaning is difference in some respect. Its original function is as a qualifier (waṣf); it is used for exception (istithnāʾ), and it necessarily requires an annexation (iḍāfa), verbal or semantic. Prefixing al- to it is an error, and it does not become definite even when annexed to a definite noun. The view of Ibn al-Sarrāj is that when the thing differing is one, it becomes definite by its annexation to it. It has been transmitted from Sibawayh that every annexation that is not pure (ghayr maḥḍa) may be intended to give definiteness, and then it becomes pure, and so ghayr becomes definite at that point with what it is annexed to, if that is definite. The detailed working out of all this is in the books of grammar.

The rhetoricians (al-bayāniyyūn) claim that ghayr or mithl, when they are the subject of a predication, are almost obligatorily placed first. They say, for example, "Your other (ghayruka) is feared for his injustice" and "Your like (mithluka) will be for noble deeds," and similar expressions in which mithl is not intended to refer to a person other than the one it is annexed to. Rather, they mean that everyone who is like him in the quality is by logical necessity and the requirement of custom expected to do what is mentioned. The poet's line:

"Other than me, most people are deceived."

His purpose is that he is not one of those who are deceived and deluded. This meaning does not hold in these two cases if they are not placed first, as in: "Your like will be for noble deeds," and "Most people are deceived other than me." You see the sentence then reversed from its proper order.

﴿Those upon whom is wrath﴾: anger (ghaḍab) is a change of disposition due to something disliked, and it may be applied to aversion (iʿrāḍ), because aversion is one of its fruits.

﴿Lā﴾ is a particle that is used for negation, for prohibition, and as a supplementary (zāʾida) particle; it is not a noun, contrary to the view of the Kufans.

﴿Nor of those who go astray﴾: al-ḍalāl means ruin and concealment: "the milk went astray in the water." It was said: its root meaning is disappearance. ﴿In a Book, my Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52]. "I lost (ḍalaltu) the thing" means I did not know the place where I had put it. "I caused the thing to go astray" (aḍlaltu al-shayʾ) means I lost it. ﴿And He causes their deeds to go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1]. "He went astray" (ḍalla) means he forgot and neglected; ﴿and I am among those who go astray﴾ [Yusuf: 20]; ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [al-Baqara: 282]. Going astray is following a course other than the intended one: "he strayed from the road" means he took a route other than its main track. Going astray is also bewilderment and hesitation, and from this is said of a smooth stone that the water moves back and forth in the valley: ḍalḍalahu. The meaning of going astray in the Qur'an has been explained as lack of knowledge of the details of matters, and as love; this will come in its places.

The genitive (jarr) in ghayr is the reading of the majority. Al-Khalil transmitted from Ibn Kathir the accusative (naṣb), and it is the reading of ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAlī and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. The genitive is then either a substitution (badal) from alladhīna, according to Abu ʿAlī, or from the pronoun in ʿalayhim; both are weak, because ghayr originally functions as a qualifier, and substitution with a qualifier is weak. Or it is a qualifier (naʿt) according to Sibawayh; in that case ghayr becomes definite by what it is annexed to, since it is definite according to what Sibawayh transmitted, in that every annexation that is not pure may become pure and so become definite, except in the attributive adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha). Or it is according to what Ibn al-Sarrāj held, since ghayr has been used for something specific, not general. Or because alladhīna is intended as a class, not particular people. They said: just as they describe the definite with the generic alif-lam by a clause. This demolishes what they had resolved upon, namely that the definite may only be qualified by the definite. I do not choose this view, and the refutation of its unsoundness is in grammar. The accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ʿalayhim, which is the preferred view, or from alladhīna, as al-Mahdawi and others said, is an error, because a circumstantial from the genitive-annexed noun whose place has no grammatical position is not permitted. Or it is an exception (istithnāʾ), as said by al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and others; it is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), since the preceding wording does not include it. al-Farrāʾ prohibited it because of the lā in ﴿nor of those who go astray﴾, and he allowed in the accusative only the circumstantial. He said: because lā is not added except when negation precedes it, as in the poet's line:

"The Messenger of God would not approve their deed, nor would the two good ones, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar."

Whoever holds the exception makes lā a connective particle (ṣila), that is, a supplementary particle like it in the words of the Exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12], and the line of the rajaz poet:

"So I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking."

And the line of al-Aḥwaṣ:

"And they blame me in play that I do not love it, while play has a persistent, unheedless caller."

al-Ṭabari said: i.e., that you mock, and that I love it. Others said: its meaning is the intention that I do not love it, so lā is in it a fixed negation, not supplementary. They also argued for its supplementary use with a verse recited by the commentators:

"His generosity refused, not avarice, and it hastened him, yes, from a youth who does not prevent generosity from killing him."

They claimed that lā is supplementary and al-bukhl is the object of abā, i.e., his generosity refused avarice. There is no proof in this; rather the more evident view is that lā is the object of abā, and that the word lā is not connected to it, and it becomes a verbal predication (isnād lafẓī). That is why he said: "it hastened him, yes," making yes the subject of "hastened," which is a verbal predication, and al-bukhl is either a substitution for lā or an object of purpose. It was said: ghayr is in the accusative by an implied verb "I mean" (aʿnī), which he attributed to al-Khalil; this is an easy estimation. ʿAlayhim is in the place of the nominative by al-maghḍūb, which is the grammatical subject of a passive verb whose agent is unspecified. Concerning the placement of the prepositional phrase in the position of the agent when it is omitted, there is disagreement mentioned in grammar. Among the subtleties of its issues is a question in which one dispenses with the predicate of the subject, mentioned in grammar.

The lā in ﴿nor of those who go astray﴾ is for emphasizing the meaning of negation, because ghayr contains negation; it is as if it were said: "Not those upon whom is wrath, nor those who go astray." It specifies its entry through the conjunction upon ﴿those upon whom is wrath﴾, because of the affinity with ghayr, and so that by omitting it one would not suppose that ﴿those who go astray﴾ is conjoined to alladhīna. ʿUmar and Ubayy read: "wa-ghayri al-ḍāllīn" (with the genitive), and it is transmitted from them that in both places the raʾ may be read in the accusative or the genitive. It indicates that those upon whom is wrath are other than those who go astray, and emphasis in it is further away, while emphasis in lā is closer. Because the meaning of ghayr is close to the meaning of lā, al-Zamakhshari brought a question to demonstrate their closeness. He said: "You say: 'I, Zayd, am other than one who strikes,' although 'I, Zayd, am like one who strikes' is impermissible, because it is equivalent to your saying 'I, Zayd, am not one who strikes.'" He means that when the governing word is genitive by annexation, its complement may not precede it or the annexed noun. But they were lenient with the governing word annexed to ghayr, so they permitted placing its complement before ghayr, treating ghayr as not being like lā. So just as the complement of what follows lā may not precede it, similarly with ghayr. Al-Zamakhshari presented it as a settled question, one finished with, in order to strengthen the correspondence between ghayr and lā, since he mentioned no disagreement in it. This view to which al-Zamakhshari went is very weak; he built it upon the permissibility of "I, Zayd, am not striking," and on the preposing of the complement of what follows lā over it there are three positions mentioned in grammar. That a word is close in meaning to another does not justify applying its rules to it, and a construction is not established except by hearing from the Arabs, and "I, Zayd, am other than striking" has not been heard. Our companions (the grammarians of our school) have mentioned the view of those who permitted this and refuted it. Some of them estimated for ﴿ghayr al-maghḍūb﴾ an implied noun, saying: the estimate is "other than the path of those upon whom is wrath," and they stated this estimate without restricting it to the genitive or accusative of ghayr. This is only possible with the accusative of ghayr, so that it would be a qualifier of "the path" (al-ṣirāṭ), and this is weak because the substitution precedes the qualifier, whereas the norm is the reverse. Or it is a qualifier of the substitution, which is ﴿the path of those﴾; or a substitution of al-ṣirāṭ, or of ﴿the path of those﴾, and this involves repeated substitution. This is an issue on which I have not found the words of anyone, except that they mentioned this in the substitution of the vocative. Or it is a circumstantial of the first or second path.

Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read: "wa-lā al-ḍaʾlīn" (with a hamza), replacing the alif with a hamza to avoid the meeting of two quiescent letters. Abu Zayd transmitted "daʾba" and "shaʾba" in the Book of Hamz, and from it came some words of this kind. Nevertheless, this substitution is not a general rule, because it did not occur frequently enough to require analogy; the grammarians stated explicitly that it is not analogical. Abu Zayd said: I heard ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recite ﴿On that day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ [al-Rahman: 39], and I thought he had made a grammatical error, until I heard from the Arabs "daʾba" and "shaʾba." Abu al-Fath said: upon this dialect is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"When the spears are reddened with fresh blood."

And the verse of another:

"As for the earth, if its blackness has become clear, and if its whiteness has become dark."

**Part 3 of 3**

In line with what Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said, that it is a dialect in which this is applicable, the bestowal of blessing is placed in the relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and the anger in the relative clause of *al* (the definite article). This is because the relative clause of *alladhina* is a verb, so its time is specific, whereas the relative clause of *al* is a noun, so its time is indefinite. The intended meaning is the request for guidance to the path of those upon whom God's blessing has been established and confirmed. For the same reason, He used the verb in the past tense and the noun in the relative clause of *anna*, so that it would encompass all times. He also used the passive form, because the one from whom guidance is requested, and to whom blessing is attributed, is not a fitting object for the attribution of anger. This is a context of gentleness, kindness and humility in seeking benevolence, so it is not appropriate to confront him with the description of retribution. Also, so that "those who have incurred anger" would serve as a preparation for ending the surah with "those who have gone astray," by conjoining one relative pronoun to another of the same kind, in agreement with the final rhymes of the verses. By "blessing" is meant religious blessing. "Those who have incurred anger" and "those who have gone astray" are general terms applying to everyone who has incurred anger and gone astray.

It has been said: "Those who have incurred anger" are the Jews, and "those who have gone astray" are the Christians. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. This was also reported from Adi ibn Hatim, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). If this is authentic, it is obligatory to adopt it. It has also been said that they are the Jews and the polytheists, and it has been said otherwise.

Some restrictions have been reported in the books of tafsir concerning anger and going astray, from the Sufis, which the wording does not indicate. Such as the saying of some of them: "﴿other than those who have incurred anger﴾" refers to neglecting good manners during the performance of service to Him, and "﴿nor of those who have gone astray﴾" refers to regarding that (service) as one's own achievement. And other things have been said besides this.

Anger from God, exalted is He, means the will to exact retribution from the disobedient, because He knows the servant before his creation and before the disobedience proceeds from him. Thus it is one of the attributes of the essence (*sifat al-dhat*, attributes belonging to the divine essence itself). Or it means the infliction of punishment upon him, and thus it is one of the attributes of action (*sifat al-af'al*, attributes pertaining to divine acts). Anger was placed before going astray, although anger is a consequence of going astray: one who strays from the truth is angered at him, and it is placed next to the blessing. The relevance of mentioning it is a correspondence, because blessing is opposed by retribution, whereas going astray is not opposed to blessing. Blessing is the conveyance of good to the one blessed, and retribution is the conveyance of harm to the one against whom anger is directed. Between them there is a semantic antithesis. There is also in it a harmony of rhyme, because His saying "﴿nor of those who have gone astray﴾" is the end of the surah, so it harmonizes with the final verses. Had anger and its object been placed later, it would not have harmonized with the final verses.

The conjunction used was the all-inclusive *wa* (and), which does not indicate precedence or subsequence, because this meaning is achieved through the difference between the two descriptions being combined: the anger directed at him and the going astray, for the one upon whom God has bestowed blessing. Even if the words are interpreted as referring to the Jews and the Christians, the precedence is either for chronological reasons or for the intensity of enmity, because the Jews are older and more intensely hostile than the Christians.

* *

In the course of the tafsir of this noble surah, many benefits from the science of eloquence (*'ilm al-bayan*) have emerged, which can only be extracted by one who has delved deeply into the understanding of the Arabic language, has been granted a generous share of the science of literature, and is knowledgeable in the elegance of speech, capable of composing graceful prose and verse. As for one who has no acquaintance with the speech of the Arabs, whose nature has become dull even to a single passage of literature, his hearing is closed to this discipline and his mind is far from this purpose.

They have said: In this noble surah there are several kinds of eloquence and rhetoric:

(The first kind): the excellence of the opening and the brilliance of the beginning. If its first verse is "﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾" according to the view of one who counts it as part of the surah, then that alone is enough excellence, since its beginning opens with the name of God. If its first verse is "﴿Praise be to God﴾," then praise of God and commendation of Him by what is worthy of Him, and describing Him with His exalted attributes, is the finest way to begin speech, and it is placed before prose and verse. The opening with praise recurs in many surahs. Openings are divided into good and bad, and the good into apparent and hidden, as has been classified in the science of rhetorical embellishment (*'ilm al-badi'*).

(The second kind): exaggeration in praise, and this is due to the generality of the definite article *al* in "praise" according to the interpretation already mentioned.

(The third kind): the shifting of discourse (*talwin al-khitab*), according to the saying of some of them. For he mentioned that "Praise be to God" has the form of a declarative statement but its meaning is a command, like His saying "﴿there is no doubt in it﴾," whose meaning is a prohibition.

(The fourth kind): specification by the *lam* in "for God" (*lillah*), since it indicates that all praises are specifically His, because He alone deserves them. And by the genitive construction in "Master of the Day of Judgment," because on that day dominion and kingdoms cease for anyone other than Him, and He alone holds sovereignty and possession. He, exalted is He, said: "﴿To whom belongs the dominion this Day?﴾" And because on that Day no one other than Him recompenses deeds.

(The fifth kind): ellipsis (*al-hadhf*). On the reading of one who puts "praise" in the accusative, it is apparent, and it has already been discussed whether it is to be supplied from the word "praise" or from something other than its wording. Some of them have said: Among it is the deletion of the governing element, which in reality is a predicate of "praise," and which is supplied as "existing" or "established." He said: Among it is the deletion of "path" in His saying "﴿other than those who have incurred anger﴾," the implied meaning being "other than the path of those who have incurred anger, and other than the path of those who have gone astray." Among it is also the deletion of "chapter" if we supply the governing element of "praise," when we put it in the accusative, as "remember" or "recite," so the implied meaning is "recite the chapter of praise." As for one who restricts "the Most Merciful," "the Most Compassionate," "we worship," "we seek help," "You have blessed," "those who have incurred anger," and "those who have gone astray," he will find many elisions in this surah.

(The sixth kind): anteriority and posteriority (*al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir*). This occurs in His saying "we worship," "we seek help," "those who have incurred anger," and "those who have gone astray." The discussion of this has already preceded.

(The seventh kind): explanation (*al-tafsir*), also called clarification after ambiguity. This occurs in the apposition of "﴿the path of those﴾" to "﴿the straight path﴾."

(The eighth kind): the shift of grammatical person (*al-iltifat*). This occurs in "﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾" and "﴿guide us﴾."

(The ninth kind): the request for something, where the intended meaning is not its attainment but its continuation. This occurs in "﴿guide us﴾."

(The tenth kind): the enumeration of attributes, to explain a particularity in the one described, or for praise or blame.

(The eleventh kind): rhymed prose (*al-taj'i*). In this surah there is parallel rhymed prose (*al-taj'i al-mutawazi*), which is the agreement of the last two words in measure and final rhyme. Examples are His saying "﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾," "﴿guide us to the straight path﴾," and His saying "﴿we seek help﴾" with "﴿nor of those who have gone astray﴾."

Our discussion of the tafsir of al-Fatiha has ended.

Al-Hasan disliked calling it "Umm al-Kitab" (the Mother of the Book), and Ibn Sirin disliked calling it "Umm al-Qur'an" (the Mother of the Qur'an), but the majority permitted it. There is consensus that it consists of seven verses, except for an anomalous view from one whose dissent is not taken into account. The Meccan and Kufan scholars of counting, the majority, counted "﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾" as a verse, but did not count "﴿those upon whom You have bestowed blessing﴾." Other counters, including Ibn Kathir among the reciters of Mecca and Kufa, did not count it as a verse, but counted "﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed blessing﴾" as a verse. Amr ibn Ubayd was anomalous in making "﴿You alone we worship﴾" a verse, so on his count it has eight verses. Husayn al-Ju'fi was anomalous in claiming it has six verses. Ibn Atiyya said: God's saying, exalted is He, "﴿We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾" is the decisive proof in this matter. They did not differ that the basmala at the beginning of every surah is not a verse, except that Ibn al-Mubarak was anomalous and said that it is a verse in every surah. I do not know what criterion is considered in the length of a verse, by which we would distinguish a verse from non-verse.

The exegetes mentioned the number of letters of al-Fatiha and mentioned a cause of its revelation that does not count as a cause of revelation. They mentioned hadiths about the virtues of "﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾," God knows best about them. They also mentioned things about the basmala that do not count as causes. They mentioned that al-Fatiha is called "al-Hamd" (the Praise), "Fatihat al-Kitab" (the Opening of the Book), "Umm al-Kitab" (the Mother of the Book), "al-Sab' al-Mathani" (the Seven Oft-Repeated), "al-Waqiya" (the Protector), "al-Kafiya" (the Sufficient), "al-Shifa" (the Cure), "al-Shafiya" (the Healing), "al-Ruqya" (the Incantation), "al-Kanz" (the Treasure), "al-Asas" (the Foundation), "al-Nur" (the Light), "Surat al-Salat" (the Surah of Prayer), "Surat Ta'lim al-Mas'ala" (the Surah Teaching the Request), "Surat al-Munaja" (the Surah of Intimate Supplication), and "Surat al-Tafwid" (the Surah of Surrender). They mentioned that the hadiths about the virtues of al-Fatiha, and all discussion of this, belong to the category of supplementary remarks (*al-tadhyilat*), and are not part of the science of tafsir, except what concerns the specification of something ambiguous, or the cause of revelation, or abrogation, by what is authentically reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Such matters are necessary for the science of tafsir. Likewise they discussed "Amin," its dialects, the disagreement over its meaning and its ruling in prayer, though it is not part of the Qur'an. Therefore we have passed over discussion of it entirely, just as we left aside discussion of the seeking of refuge (*al-isti'adha*) at the beginning of the book. Exegetes have lengthened their books with matters outside the science of tafsir, which we have omitted from this book of ours, since our aim is what we indicated in the introduction. And God, exalted is He, knows best.
